utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, registrar. Today we are Monday, the 17th of March, 2008. I should like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people assisting us during this pre-trial -- pre-trial hearing with a view to resuming the proceedings when the Defence will call its witnesses. With this in mind, we have handed down a decision on the 22nd of February, 2008, and on the agenda we have written in ten items. I shall get back to this later, because in the meantime I shall read out an oral decision which the Trial Chamber will hand down orally today as follows: Pertaining to the Praljak Defence motions, pertaining to the protective measures of the witnesses they wish to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this decision has to do with protective measures, we shall hand down this decision in private session. Registrar, for a few minutes let's move back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session on the agenda we have the item pertaining to the opening statements of Defence counsel under Rule 84 for the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I shall give each Defence counsel the floor so that he or she can let us know how they wish to proceed. Once we have looked into this issue I shall address the second item on the agenda, which is undoubtedly the most important, namely the one which pertains to the time required by the Defence teams to present their case and the -- how the time will be broken down between the various Defence teams. So this is a crucial item as far as today's hearing's concerned. Third item, the time allocation for the cross-examination of Defence witnesses. On the one hand for the Prosecution, and on the other hand for the accused. So item 3 ties into item 2 as everybody can see. Item 4, the number of expert witnesses, of viva voce witnesses, 92 bis witnesses, and 92 ter witnesses and 92 quater witnesses that the Defence intends to call to testify. Item 5, presentation by the Defence of common witnesses. Let me give you an example: Expert witnesses, for instance. Item 6, Rule 85 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, an accused is entitled to testify, and this Rule applies. We know that Mr. Praljak has every intention of testifying. Item 7, translation deadlines and deadlines of disclosure of expert reports. Item 8, the statements provided under Rule 98(2) bis and 92 ter. Ninth item, translation of documents on the list on the 65 ter (G) list. Item 10, the obligation to disclose the document set figure on the 65 ter list (G) in hard copy to the Trial Chamber in the form of binders in the same way that the Prosecution has done when it presented its case. And if we have any further time, item 11, miscellaneous. A number of other questions can be addressed at that point in time. First item, therefore, Rule 84 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel let me tell you that before the presentation of -- by the Prosecution of its case, each party can make a statement and an opening statement. However, the Defence can decide to make its statement after the Prosecution has presented its case and before presenting its own opening statements. Therefore, Rule 84 enables the Defence team to make their opening statements before calling their witnesses to testify. In addition, Rule 84 bis, which ties into this Rule also, which entitles an accused to make a statement. As far as item 1 is concerned, I think the best would be to start with Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the court. Let me say that the Prlic Defence does not intend to give an opening statement. We don't think that it would be of any particular use to the Trial Chamber at this point with the proceedings given that we've been at it for two years. During many of the objections that were raised by the Prosecution there have been some responses which in my opinion have informed the Trial Chamber quite adequately what the Defence of the -- the Prlic Defence is all about, and therefore it would not necessarily add anything, particularly since opening statements are not evidence. Had I been before a jury, I would have given an opening statement right after the Prosecution. However, I think that in this case one is not necessary. In order to give guidance to the Court, I suspect that by the time we do begin, in light of the last scheduling that we have set, I believe it's on April 21st, by that point and with our filings on the 65(G), I believe, you will have ample notice as far as the structure of the Defence case, how we intend to proceed, how it's broken down, and that will be sufficient to -- to inform you all that there is to know about the Defence case. Of course if the Trial Chamber does wish to hear an opening statement we could put something together, but I don't think -- I think it's best to just begin hearing evidence. That's why we're all here. We want to be as efficient as possible and we want to make sure that we provide you with the information necessary for your deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I shall give the floor to other Defence counsel, but before I do that, before we move on to the second item, the Trial Chamber will address another topic which was not on the agenda for today which is also an important item which relates to the order in which the accused intend to call their witnesses. Will this be D1, D2, D3, D4, D5? Will it be in this order? What kind of order will there be? It is important that we look into this matter. Also, another question which could be addressed under this item, i.e., to know when the witnesses from the various Defence teams are called could there not be a representation on a municipality- by-municipality basis and a detention centres or camps, and if -- and other witnesses if need be? My colleague would like to take the floor and then I will give the floor back to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to make a little commentary to this suggestion. If we have one Defence team after the other, it is well possible that in May a witness for the Prlic Defence speaks of an event in Prozor, and in December a witness for the Petkovic Defence will testify about the very same event, and it will be more difficult, of course, for the Chamber then to link this immediately and to get an adequate vue d'ensemble, an adequate picture. On the other hand, the Chamber is quite aware of the fact that it will not always be possible to link a witness to one event alone and that the borders are in a way not -- not quite impenetrable. So that there is also another aspect to it which the Chamber sees. I think the work of the Chamber and also the effectiveness of the -- presenting the Defence case would rather be enhanced if you could decide on following this second alternative proposal, yet we are also aware of the fact that it will cause difficulties. For you it needs more coordination, and we are -- we are by no way at this point taking any decision on this matter, but it is our rather strong belief that it is something worth of considering, and perhaps we can have an answer when we meet again on Wednesday of the next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you wanted to take the floor again, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly. I know that my colleagues have been busy in the field, I know I have been, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that we will endeavour to -- to do what is best. And we'll see if we can assist the Trial Chamber in the manner in which you have suggested. However, I have to be very candid. There should be no illusion that the Defences are getting along or will be getting along throughout the defence case. I can't guarantee that. I can only guarantee that I am willing to move heaven and earth to get my colleagues to work with me. They, on the other hand, may think that I'm working in the wrong direction and may not necessarily wish to -- and I very well may be working in the wrong direction, and so there's no need for them to following me. I can share with the Trial Chamber how I have broken down my case thus far, because we have done some calculations. We know approximately how much time we will need and the manner in which we want to present the case, and of course I haven't spoken to -- I spoke to one of my colleagues. I haven't spoken with the others. But it's in a thematic approach, and I'm willing to share that with everyone in open session in court. I don't think that's going to be a problem. I have to also caution the Trial Chamber that getting witnesses comitted to come at a particular time is rather difficult and since we moved under the assumption that we were going to go first, we've been working around the clock on this issue and sort of guesstimating when the witnesses will be coming. Again, I don't want the Trial Chamber to think that we're being obstructive or intransigent. I'm willing to work with my colleagues. I know that we have some common witness that we can share. My personal opinion is that certain witnesses should come at a particular time because it tells the narrative that is necessary for you to follow as opposed to having it in a disjunctive format. I've impressed that upon my colleagues. Of course they also represent clients, and all of my colleagues have to take certain amount of instructions from their clients. Though, I would say that it doesn't matter when a particular witness comes, it shouldn't matter to the client that is, but it will matter in the narrative. I've constructed a narrative for you. So, in any event, at some point I can proceed and tell you exactly how we have constructed our case which I believe makes the most appropriate sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We will now proceed. This hearing is a good opportunity for everyone to speak their minds, so let me say that after my fellow Judge who mentioned Prozor, I could mention Mostar. Let's assume for example that one of you calls witnesses to call about shelling or sniping incidents in Mostar. Let's assume that we have a witness who comes to testify about this in December. Then let's assume that seven months later another Defence team calls another witness to talk about sniping in Mostar. Of course the Trial Chamber is perfectly able to go back to these incidents, but it would be far better if the same subjects would be dealt with at the same time by everyone for us to then move on to a different subject. But Mr. Karnavas has said that sometimes there are scheduling problems to deal with, problems then also related to the individual strategies of each Defence team, and that such an approach will not always be feasible. We'll see that you have to tell us about this, each and every one of you. Now we'll proceed with respect to Rule 84. The Prlic Defence has told us that they would not be making an opening statement. Let me move on to Defence team D2. Who will take the floor for D2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. There -- it is anticipated that an opening statement will be made by the Stojic Defence. It will not, looking quite far ahead, be very long, probably an hour, an hour and a half in duration, but of course it will be made, if it is made at all, at prior to the first witness for Bruno Stojic being called. In other words, after the Prlic case has been closed. So, Your Honour, that's very shortly that matter dealt with. Your Honour, I think of course one always gives the most anxious scrutiny and careful thought to any proposal put forward by Your Honours. In relation to the proposal adumbrated by His Honour Judge Trechsel, I have two observations with your leave. The first is that at this stage, and I stand to be corrected by my learned leader, it's not anticipated that the Stojic will call many witnesses if any dealing with the municipality-by-municipality approach, so I don't think it's really going to be relevant to us, but Your Honours of course have dealt with many cases and are extremely experienced, but caution always had to be had over managing cases. For example, it may well have been the case, for example, that my learned friend - and it may not concern us - but as friend of the Court as it were, the Prlic case may call a particular witness dealing with a particular location. And if the cases were taken out of order, the next witness, of course, could easily, dealing with the same municipality, put forward a completely different narrative. Now, of course rather than helping Your Honours, that could complicate not just the factual understanding of the case but also poison the atmosphere of the courtroom because perhaps one accused would feel that he's not being given a fair shot at putting a particular case forward. Your Honours, of course it's a matter for each counsel and at the end of the day every counsel has an obligation to put the case in the best interests of the client, but in that as well it's a matter of persuading Your Honours that the case has merit. So it doesn't -- and it's not anticipated that any counsel conducting who is conducting a case diligently will seek to irritate Your Honours by unnecessary -- unnecessarily calling witnesses. I think the best rule of thumb would be, in my respectful submission, that if a witness called by another accused satisfactorily deals with a particular area of testimony, the -- the accuseds that are coming afterwards perhaps don't need to call that witness covering that same area at all. And that's the logical common sense approach that one would hope would be adopted. But, Your Honours, of course it can be kept under review and matters may be a little clearer when the 65 ter summaries are given at the end of the month, perhaps a more informed decision can be taken then by all of us. Your Honour, did you want to go on to the areas of the time needed for the Defence and the number of witnesses or will Your Honour deal with that -- Mr. President deal with that later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on. We'll come back to this later on. Thank you. To sum up, the Stojic Defence is considering making an opening statement of between an hour and an hour and a half. Let me now move on to Mr. Praljak's Defence. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. My fellow Judge has a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sorry. I just want to make sure that I have understood correctly. Mr. Khan has said that he -- if the Stojic Defence make an opening statement, that will be after the presentation of the Prlic case. Is that correct? Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour's quite right. That's exactly what we propose and that's the normal way that operates in -- well, in many courts, but particularly the ICTY. Your Honour, my learned friend has pulled me up on one issue. Of course the timing of the opening statement is flexible at this stage. It may be longer. I'm not seeking to bind ourselves at this moment. It's an approximation. It may be longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom. Your Honours, with respect to these two matters I'll be brief. First as regards the proposal introduced today with regard to the order of witnesses. I don't want to add anything special. Nothing special to add to what Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Khan have already said. I completely agree with what they said. I'd just like to add that there's another question here, another matter that could make matters a little more difficult in the matter of coordination with that kind of approach, and that is that in this trial we have six accused. Each of them have their individual Defence counsel and Defence teams and defence case, so of course not all the Defence teams can have the same strategy, which makes life more difficult. So this coordination is something we should look at with the presentation of evidence according to different blocks, although I do agree that it is a method that I think would be a good one; and I'm certain that as far as the Defence is concerned it would be made more difficult and make work impossible at certain points unless that is done. And I'd like to underline what Mr. Khan mentioned a moment ago. I think that all the Defence teams are wise enough to see that if the first, second, and third Defence teams presents enough evidence about an event in a given location, for example Prozor was mentioned, then probably the fourth and fifth Defence teams won't have to go back to that issue. But when we bear in mind the different functions and posts held by the accused at the relevant time, then maybe, yes, because some people will find the military aspects of a matter more interesting than civil and political ones and vice versa. So you might have a situation where the witnesses are indeed testifying about the same location at the same time, but not the same aspects or the same details of certain particular events and so on and so forth. There are a number of elements that must be taken into consideration. I don't think I need to specify them all here and now. And perhaps we ought to link this up with the following: The introduction of witnesses under Rule 92 bis, for instance. My Defence team has some ambitious plans. Let me say that at the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think it would be far better if we followed the agenda, because if you start talking about 92 bis witnesses, then -- which is something that is at item 8 of the agenda, it's going to be very confusing. I think we should stick to the issue of opening statements under Rule 84 or to the issue of Rule 84 bis, possible opening statements by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, and I apologise for not being clear enough, explicit enough. I didn't want to deal with 92 bis. That's a separate question on the agenda, but I just wanted to mention that that is an instrument which will in a way be combined in the order of the presentation of evidence, for example. And if the first Defence team brings witnesses in to testify about Prozor, there's no reason why the third Defence team should make a proposal under 92 bis since we've heard the viva voce witness and some repetitions, repetitive statements. And perhaps this would be very useful, because if the 92 bis witness passes through the courtroom, I know that I need not bring him in again. Or if the proposal is rejected, I will have to recall the same witness at some later date, and so on and so forth. So that's what I wanted to illustrate. That there are a lot of pros and cons. Now, as far as your request about the opening statements is concerned, yes, the Defence of General Praljak does intend to have an opening statement pursuant to Rule 84 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the supplemental, the opening statements of the accused under Rule 84 bis, and we shall of course coordinate all this. We won't be speaking about the same thing. It's difficult for me to specify about a time. We're making some drafts, but let me say that I don't think we'll need more than two, to two and a half hours. That's how things stand at present. Of course I do have the right to make the statement and like the -- my learned friend I consider that that opening statement should be made when the 3D Defence starts, not at the very beginning. So that is when I would like to have that statement delivered. And I think that the opening statement can be a mild -- of mild assistance to the Chamber to help them understand before the Defence case goes ahead. And along those same lines, General Praljak would also like to make a statement. Let me just remind you, and I'm sure you're fully conscious of that, that he'll rule -- use Rule 84 bis at the beginning and the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, at the request of Mr. Praljak, to deal with Rule 88 bis said that General Praljak could ask for an additional statement under Rule 84 bis bearing in mind the practice and the text of 84 bis, Rule 84 bis, I will be making a written submission or written request, or I can do so orally today or at the next session, whichever you prefer. So those are our responses to the two matters raised. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. You're talking about two hours, two hours and a half. Does that include your opening statement and Mr. Praljak's statement? Is that right? So in total you and Mr. Praljak will need between two and two and a half hours? Is that the way we should understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think -- I said it, but I don't think it was translated specifically. I think that for both that would be a reasonable time. Whether it's two hours or three hours I can't say at present, and I'll probably be able to be more precise at the next Status Conference, but I have a first draft. I'm working on my initial draft and trying to see what we should do before the case begins for you to be able to follow the case better, and of course I haven't had detailed discussions with General Praljak yet. I do know some of his ideas, but I think that about two and a half hours would be the right time. So whether it's going to be half an hour longer or shorter, that's a rough estimate, but by the next meeting I'm sure that I'll be able to be more precise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A technical point first. On page 18, first line, you are quoted and correctly so as referring to Rule 88 bis, but I suppose you wanted to say 84 bis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct, 84 bis. That's right, Judge Trechsel. And as far as I can see, it's been changed in the meantime. So it is 84 bis throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and by way of comment you're quite right, the Chamber is aware of the fact that your client has made a very lengthy full day statement in the beginning, and when he was promised the opportunity to take the floor again, the Chamber will reserve its right to limit the time in view of the fact that it is in a way a second go, which is not as such foreseen in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to General Petkovic. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, good afternoon. The -- as far as Rule 84 is concerned, the position is that, yes, the Petkovic Defence would wish to make an opening statement in the same way as indicated by Mr. Khan. We propose to make that at the beginning of our case after -- well, it would be the first three Defence cases. So far as the estimate is concerned, it is slightly premature. I'm sure Your Honours will understand clearly we're talking hours, not days, and Your Honours wouldn't really allow us days anyway, but that's -- it's into the sensible, really, to attempt any sort of firm estimate at the moment. And so far as 84 bis is concerned, that's very simple, Your Honour. General Petkovic himself does not propose to make any statement or request to make any statement under 84 bis. So far as the very interesting suggestion floated by His Honour Judge Trechsel is concerned, naturally Your Honours would expect us to take time as we all will to think about this and consider it. Just a couple of observations at this point. Our immediate reaction, and we've had such discussions we've been able to have very quickly, our immediate reaction is -- is to see that there may very well turn out to be more difficulties in than are actually solved and everybody, and I can see from Judge Trechsel's reaction, everybody's receptive to that problem but we'll consider it. There are a couple of maybe relatively minor difficulties, one -- perhaps not a major one, but if we do do that it does have the effect of potentially Defences calling some of their witnesses before they make their opening statement under 84; that's not the biggest point in the case but it is a feature. Possibly of more practical significance is, and this follows from some of the discussions we've already had, but if we were talking about, let's say a Petkovic witness for Prozor let's say, rather than have such a witness scheduled to follow immediately after, let's say, Mr. Karnavas, whether he's got some, but Mr. Karnavas's witness on Prozor, it -- in the end may be more satisfactory if we consider in the light of that evidence and reflect upon whether that witness is actually needed, it's slightly more likely that witnesses would be brought unnecessarily if we have to schedule them municipality by municipality in accordance with what I'll call Judge Trechsel's suggestion, just to give it a label, as opposed to thinking about it as we go along because it is very likely in practice that a consideration and reflection upon evidence given in relation to particular municipalities or particular areas will lead Defence cases to say well, we don't need this we don't need that and so on. So Your Honours at this point those are all our observations but of course there may be more to come from future hearings after reflection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not mind this labelling, but I want to recall that it is in fact the Chamber's suggestion on which I have a bit elaborated, but it's the Chamber's suggestion. But you may call it the Trechsel suggestion, because it may make things easier to identify because the Chamber has many suggestions and I have very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's -- credit where credit is due I always say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. At this stage the D4 Defence has not given any time for its opening statement. Let me remind you that as far as I remember, in the cases before this Tribunal opening statements never went over one day or, let's say, two days of hearing. And here I'm thinking of the Milosevic case, although I'm not even certain about that. The Chamber will look into the matter, into opening statements in other cases to see about the time, because of course you could imagine an opening statement that could last for weeks, but at some point the Trial Chamber has to set limits, time limits. The Trial Chamber will look back at all the trials and see how long opening statements have been in the past. Let me now move on to D5. You have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. The Defence of Mr. Coric intends to present an opening statement. And as Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic's Defences have stated, we will also do this at the beginning of our case. It would be about one hour long, and the purpose of the opening statement is to indicate to the Chamber what we intend to show during our presentation of evidence what our case is, to make it easier for Your Honours to follow the evidence. And in accordance with this, my comment on the Trial Chamber's proposal about the order in which evidence will be presented is as follows: I agree with everything my colleagues have already said, so I will not repeat it now, but I wish to add one thing. Our Defence case is such that it is not necessarily arranged by municipality. Our witnesses will not be linked to particular municipalities necessarily, and some of them will testify to events in more than one municipality. This complicates our situation considerably if we were to follow the order suggested and if we have to come after witnesses testifying to one particular municipality. What I wish to say about everyone calling their witnesses within their own Defence case is the following: If witnesses of previous Defence teams testified to events that one of our witnesses will testify to, our witness will either not testify to those events or we will not call the witness at all. This will expedite the proceedings and shorten the time needed for our Defence case. That was in brief what I wished to say. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. To sum up, D5 thinks of making an opening statement that would last about one hour. Let me finish by turning to the D6 Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Pusic's Defence wishes to retain the right to make an opening statement at the beginning of our case. It will last an hour and a half at the most. If we decide not to make an opening statement after all, we will notify the Trial Chamber and everybody else on time, and it will therefore save us time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now we have a very clear picture. D1, no opening statement; D2, yes; D3, yes; D4, yes; D5, yes; D6, yes, maybe, not quite sure yet. But if it's yes, then they'll need an hour and a half. Whilst listening to all of you, I've found out something I was not aware of, and that you've sort of come to an agreement and that the Prlic Defence will start. If I understand, the Prlic Defence will go first with the presentation of its case, followed by D2, D3, D4, D5, and D6. Mr. Karnavas, is that the way we should understand the position? I'm giving you the floor, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in all the cases that I've ever tried in my career, and there have been some, it's always been -- that's been the procedure unless it can be agreed upon. Normally the Prosecution indicts in a hierarchical order. We heard Mr. Scott say that's not the case in this case, but that's intellectually dishonest. In this case they've indicted in a particular hierarchical order with Dr. Prlic being where he is given his position, which is why at the beginning of the trial some two years ago we were maintaining that it would be best to have the cross-examination in the order in which the indictment was formatted and for the lawyers to decide who should go first as opposed to the musical chair approach, as I call it, of one person -- one day it's Prlic, the next day is Stojic. But in any event, to me it makes sense that whoever is indicted first goes first. It clarifies it. It just so happens in this case if you look at the way that the indictment is formatted, that there should be no other way. Of course, I would gladly go last, gladly, although I'm sure that my colleagues would prefer me going first. And I'm only saying that by going last we have more time to prepare, but that's the way it is. But in -- since you've asked me that question, it should also be noted, that since we are going first, in light of the way the indictment is drafted, at least the way when we get down to -- when we start discussing hours and witnesses and what have you, I should note that we have taken it upon ourselves to construct our defence in a manner in which the first half of the defence deals with the global issues related to the joint criminal enterprise, those sorts of aspects, which obviously will assist everybody in the Defence, or it may not, I mean, they may have their own way of doing things, but in any event, I will be disclosing the names of all my witnesses to them well in advance. You know, even today so they can look at it. And if they wanted to introduce some of those -- some of their witnesses that go to those aspects during that period, we would welcome that. We think that makes sense. And I know that there are some other witnesses that certain Defence lawyers wish to call that we believe should come in earlier because it will assist the Trial Chamber. Not because they assist Prlic, but the Trial Chamber. And that's why we should -- they should come in earlier. So in any event, that's -- I hope I have answered your question, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are very clear indeed. Yes, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, everybody in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, I just want to make a limited intervention at this stage. And in the absence of Mr. Scott and Mr. Stringer, who have notified why they couldn't be here today, I do have to make a note that at page 24, line 2, there is an accusation of intellectual dishonesty, and basically that Mr. Scott -- and I don't think he would take kindly to that. I think that's unnecessary. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll just leave it, but in essence to suggest that somehow there wasn't a particular order, it flies in the face of logic. You know, maybe it's too harsh to say dishonesty. I should have said maybe something else. But it does fly in the face of logic. And let's be adult about this, and I think Mr. Kruger knows what I'm talking about. But I accept - and I don't mean to offend Mr. Scott - but if he was here I probably would say the same thing in his face. I don't want him to think that I'm speaking behind his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May we just observe, we're not going to say anything about how the order in the indictment was chosen, but simply to say that yes, we concur that unless there was some agreement among the Defence teams that had had the Trial Chamber's endorsement and approval, we should just stick to D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6. That's the Petkovic Defence position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Relating to this issue, the Chamber had no particular opinion. You decide. It could be D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6. It is the order as you wish it to be. We as Trial Chamber have no major input in this matter. So we take due note of the fact that you'd rather keep the order as in the indictment, D1 to D6. But it -- had you suggested something else, we would have agreed to it. Very well. We've dealt with item 1. Let's move on to item 2. Personally, and I think this is also the view of my colleagues, it is the most crucial item in our agenda since it deals with the time requested by the Defence for the presentation of their evidence. Also, as to the way this time is going to be spread amongst the various Defence teams. For the time being, the Trial Chamber has no document whatsoever. We're not aware of your summaries or witnesses. We don't know anything, but I guess you've already started working on your Defence, rather more than less, I should say, so I suppose that you have some ideas -- yes, some ideas to convey to us. Let us begin with Mr. Karnavas. Let's follow the order starting with D1. Mr. Karnavas, in this respect what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All right. As far as the time to present the evidence, here's how I have it: The total of approximately 165 hours. Now, of that, approximately 70 hours would be what I would call witnesses that go -- that are common witnesses, that deal with various issues. And I would also say that probably some 44 hours also deal with issues that are related to everybody, although perhaps not as much. But I would say that half of the hours go to what I would call the JCE issues. Now, of that period of time, I should also note, I'm going to move ahead of the schedule a little bit, because it is on the schedule about the testimony of the accused, with your permission I would cover that. The 165 hours also includes what we believe would be an estimated period of time for in which Dr. Prlic will be providing evidence. In other words, what we believe the time it would take for direct examination. Okay? Keeping in mind, as far as I understand, that normally Trial Chambers are reluctant to put a specific time limitation on the testimony in which an accused, you know, gives. Of course, there's -- the Trial Chamber does have the right to restrict the testimony of any witness, including the accused, if that testimony is not relevant, it's repetitive, it's not assisting. So -- but we believe that a certain amount of time is going to be necessary. So in any event, that's how we've broken it down. To be more concrete, dealing with issues what we call with the Croatia Republic, for approximately 24 hours we're looking at dealing with issues at the state level. For a variety of issues that we believe are necessary and are inclusive in the indictment approximately 30 horse. Issues dealing with the HVO, HZ, HB, or HR HB together, we believe with the -- excluding Dr. Prlic's testimony, approximately 44 hours. Of course some of that can change. There's some miscellaneous witnesses which we believe are -- will cover approximately 23 to 25 hours. We have some expert witnesses that again these expert witnesses go to everyone, not to any particular accused such as Dr. Prlic. We've taken it upon ourselves. We took the initiative early on. We believe that they would be essential to the various issues in the court -- in this case, dealing with the JCE, approximately 15 hours. We have three particular experts at this time. And then we have some other witnesses that would directly relate -- directly relate, virtually exclusively, I should say, to Dr. Prlic, and they go to character witness. So -- I don't believe in playing games and hiding the ball and we're going to be here for a long time. They're going to get the list in two weeks so it doesn't really matter. And I just think that for scheduling purposes it helps everybody to know that that's how we've broken it down. So it would be our proposal that we would start dealing with the issues of Croatia, Tudjman, and what have you, the refugee issues that go there. Then dealing with the issues of the state, the Presidency, international negotiations with the state, those issues. Then, as I said, HVO, the Croatian Community, Croatian republic. And it would be our suggestion, Your Honours, I'll be very frank, normally I know that in some jurisdictions they would prefer to have the accused testify first. I don't that there is any particular rule of thumb. It would be our intention, and we would hope that the Trial Chamber would understand and not try to deduct any weight as a result of Dr. Prlic coming at any particular time, that it would not be until we get to that portion; that is, dealing with the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that at that point we would have Dr. Prlic testify first and foremost with the rest of the witnesses following after that. So in other words, we would have some common witnesses above, and then at some point we would formally commence with our case, as it were, specific to Dr. Prlic, you know, even though many of the issues will be assisting the other accused in the sense that they're tied into this whole notion of the joint criminal enterprise. As far as the experts are concerned, again depending on where they fit best, we believe perhaps at least one if not two of them would be at the early phase. One would be at the latter, although I'm moving with all deliberate speed to have all of them prepared to go during the first phase of -- that is before we get to the Prlic specific Defence case. So I think that's what we have. Now, I should also note that there are two particular witnesses, one expert and then another witness, that we will be sharing in a sense with other Defence and there may be others, I don't know what their list of witnesses are, but there's one particular expert and there is another one. And let me raise this issue right now while I'm on my feet: I'm concerned that when we -- when we decide how many hours to give to a particular witness that it is necessary for the Defence, the lawyers, in advance to try to determine among themselves if they have any what I would call positive evidence to elicit from that particular witness. It may be that one Defence team is calling a witness, but that witness I wish to extract a certain amount of evidence. Not cross-examine but direct evidence in a sense, and here's where the dilemma might lie: Let's just say team X calls this witness and only wishes to examine the witness for one hour. However, because of where the -- the witness may have potential information that assists not just my client but may go to the joint criminal enterprise, and I might need six hours with that witness for direct examination or others may need as well in order to cover all of it, if -- if that were the case, the Trial Chamber is put in a dilemma as the Defence, because I cannot cross-examine somebody in 15 or 20 minutes or one hour, my time divided by six, the cross-examination time, and cover all those topics. We don't want to be in a position where we're fighting over witnesses. And a witness belongs to the court. It doesn't belong to any particular individual. So there maybe instances as I said, that a witness may be called by a particular Defence team that might have been called earlier or for whatever reason was not, and in that case there must be some flexibility where a particular Defence that wishes to also conduct some direct examination should alert the Court that they will require X amount of time and here are the reasons. And of course non-repetitive. It's got to be relevant. So I think that's just the fairest approach to take and I just put that out. I don't know if there is anything else the Court wishes for me to address at this point. I've come here fully prepared today to answer all questions depending -- based on your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, sorry. This is a very interesting proposition indeed, which is to examine a witness called by another Defence team, but I do have one concern. In such a case would the witness be part of your witness list? Would he be -- would the list be given to the Chamber beforehand, or is the Chamber going to be taken by surprise to learn that you have actually a new witness? I mean, through this witness that you want to examine in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. First of all, I don't believe that trial by ambush or surprising anybody assists anyone. In fact, I think that -- I often say that a lawyer in court has one reputation to lose in his entire career, not per case. So I think the best approach is to be quite honest and forthright with the Trial Chamber. Their style may -- you know, may differ, but in any event, I would like to think that I've been very honest with this Trial Chamber throughout the proceedings. It would be my intention to notify, even before the commencement of the trial, of the Defence case, that here are some witnesses. These are the issues. We're sharing this witness so that there are no surprises. I don't think that they -- you know, now, there may be, for instance, a case, I don't think that it's going to be likely, but there may be, for instance, a case where a particular witness might have some additional information that wasn't -- that we weren't cognisant of prior to the commencement, in which case I would say -- I would ask for leave in advance and say, "Well, Your Honours, I didn't have that information," albeit being due diligent, but I would suspect that with all of my colleagues, once we've seen each other's lists, and we haven't seen them yet, we would know in advance. It's pretty difficult not to see a list and not to see the documents and not figure out what those people are going to say. At least if you've been prepared and working on this case all along. So it's going to be pretty clear why the witness is called and what they're going to be saying. And so -- and that will be even more apparent as of March 31st. So -- but I don't believe in surprises, and I don't think that the Trial Chamber would expect surprises from the lawyers. I mean, maybe you would, you know -- we would be more than happy to surprise you occasionally and maybe come in a congenial personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would say a little bit of suspense and surprise doesn't harm, I would say. What I would find important is that amongst the teams you inform and warn each other that Witness 75 is one I want another hour of so that the scheduling can be made accordingly, the amount of time needed for the witness. This, I think, is important in order to avoid being squeezed suddenly, lack of time for one witness, the next witness waiting already. I think for this purpose some coordination would be useful, and I'm sure you agree with that to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree with that and I think that that should be something more -- perhaps said even more forcefully and that it is expected upon us to do that. Now, during the course of the proceedings, of course, evidence may come out where all of a sudden now may have to go into a particular issue that you weren't aware of or you hadn't anticipated, and you may need to readjust and again in those instances it would be up to us to ask for leave, provide you with the information and then for you to make the determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas if I understood you properly, because I listened to you religiously when you spoke, here are the conclusions would I draw: You basically envisage 165 hours, out of which 70 would be devoted to common witnesses who would be of interest to all the other accused. There would be 44 hours devoted to witnesses who would deal with topics that also are of interest to the other teams. You also said that Mr. Prlic was going to testify. So if I add it all up, if I'm not mistaken, you plan Mr. Prlic's testimony to last at least 60 hours? If I take it out, 165 minus 70, minus 44; so there would be some 60 hours for Mr. Prlic's testimony. And you announced the basic themes that would be covered, Tudjman, Croatia, the Presidency, international negotiations, the HVO, the HR HB, et cetera. That's very good, because this shows us clearly all the topics you want to deal with. And you said, and I was very surprised to hear that, you said that as part of the 165 hours at some point in time Dr. Prlic, your client, was going to testify, and that you would continue then, once he was done, with witnesses. Maybe with common witnesses or witnesses likely to be of interest to other teams. So I'm a little taken aback. Are you going to fit in his testimony among -- within the general time? You know that if Dr. Prlic is to testify he's going to be asked questions by the Judges. That goes without saying. Questions in order to have no surprises based on exhibits, Prosecution exhibits and Defence exhibits, based also on documents that you are going to submit to the witness. So we're going to ask questions of him. But once he has testified, if you plan to call further witnesses, we won't be able to ask Dr. Prlic any further questions that would arise from answers provided by your other witnesses or from documents related to such witnesses. As a rule, in the history of this Tribunal accused testify in the end. That's the rule. In this way it is possible to really address all the topics and have a comprehensive view of the case. If you were to call Dr. Prlic in the middle of your Defence case we would not be able to put questions to him. Sometimes it could be questions for his benefit, of course, but you could deprive us of this right to ask questions while the accused has decided to testify, unless the Trial Chamber -- that's not provided for in the Rules, unless the Trial Chamber wants to ask questions of the accused. So this is my personal concern regarding the structure you have. My other concern, I'll give you the floor in a minute, my other concern is the number of hours. I remind you that the Prosecution used for their case 294 hours. So you speak of 165. So that's two-thirds basically of the Prosecution case, which, too, may give cause for concern. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Based on my calculation of the hours, I just note that I had noted that Dr. Prlic would testify. I didn't give a specific number, but if we do the breakdown, and perhaps my math is wrong, but he's calculated to approximately 24 hours on direct examination. Now, again these are just sort of estimates. We're trying to do our best to try to figure out -- and of course that would be because of where he --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karnavas please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and that's because of where we had him to testify. Now, as far as whether somebody goes first in the middle or last, normally that's left up to the Defence. There are some Judges in this Tribunal, and I was shocked to hear this, where they said that unless the accused testifies first, they will give little weight to their evidence because the assumption is that the accused has heard all the other evidence and now he's going to confabulate or perhaps confabulate or adjust his testimony based on the evidence. So there's that extreme. Having Dr. Prlic testify last, of course, there is something that I would have to consult with Dr. Prlic, but I don't see there to be a problem. I certainly don't want to leave the Trial Chamber with any impression that we're trying to limit the Trial Chamber of its ability to ask questions. I've constructed in this fashion based on my experience, or lack thereof, and based on the narrative, because I thought perhaps it might be -- it might be more appropriate. However, I don't see there to be a problem, and I will -- Dr. Prlic has listened to the Trial Chamber's observations and we will consult, but that won't be a problem. If the Trial Chamber wishes to hear him last in this particular case, we will give it strong consideration. So I hope that the Trial Chamber doesn't get the impression that somehow I'm trying to sneak him in some place, because it's kind of difficult to do that. But in any event, we can make some adjustments, Your Honours, in view of your -- and by the way, I should note that I really appreciate the Trial Chamber's observations in this instance because all these judicial hints obviously help me to adjust the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another observation which is one of mine, because we have not spoken about it in the Trial Chamber. This is something that crosses my mind. You may know this. You may not. I'm probably the Judge that has been sitting on most cases in international criminal justice because I have been sitting non-stop for basically four years, so I do claim to know the way international criminal justice operates. The fact that he would testify as the first witness, because also he is accused of liability under Article 7(3), which is not just something you can sweep out of the way. Article 7(3), that's command responsibility, as you know, and in case he might be accused of comitting crimes under that Article of the Statute, an issue arises. That's the degree of liability. If he were to testify first, it would not be possible for the Judges to put questions to him regarding his subordinates who might claim that their superior was warned, failed to do anything, did not check. And the fact that Dr. Prlic would testify first would not enable your client to give his view to the Trial Chamber. So here I can anticipate a problem which is not major one but that could arise. I listened to you very carefully, and you said that in this Tribunal as a rule Trial Chambers follow the order as per the indictments. That is so, but in civil law countries, including in France, generally in criminal cases it is the one that has a higher position that will testify last. So it's another scale. We start with the lowest rung, and you end with the highest rung, as it were. So it's up to you, of course, but I do observe that the fact that he would testify first and that he would testify while you are calling your witnesses might bring about some problems. With regard to common themes or to common witnesses, fine. Fine. That's -- of course that's quite crucial. And remember, at the Status Conference in nearly two years ago I had reminded you that as far as I was concerned, the Defence teams were to really discuss among themselves in order precisely to call common witnesses in order to avoid having repetitive witnesses. And I told you that when doing so you may have common witnesses presenting no problems who could be called. But there could be witnesses produced by one party who may be such that other Defence teams would have to ask questions of him or her, because such common witnesses, unfortunately so, may one turn out to be Prosecution witnesses even though they may be called by a Defence team, hence the need for cross-examination. It is all very complicated. You yourself are extremely experienced in this matter. You know that as well as I do. But given that these topics are extremely complicated, the light is seen when Defence counsel have met, and having met can identify points of agreement and disagreement. And then if you have agreement among yourselves, it is easier to have collectively witnesses who are going to say the same thing for all teams. Of course if we're talking about disagreements, then you have to call your own witnesses team by team, because one witness for one team can turn out to be a witness against another team. So that's where the problem lies. For the time being we have no idea of who is going to come as witnesses. We don't know where we're going, where we're heading for. We will know that when we have your witnesses' names, but so far nothing. But we know how much time you will need. We know the topics you're going to deal with, but we don't have any witnesses' names. Do you have anything to say before we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The only thing I can say, Your Honour, is that I take it from -- first of all, I appreciate your observations. Again, Mr. Prlic -- Dr. Prlic was placed in that order because of our own fear that if he didn't testify at a particular point - and this would be the beginning of our case - that there may be some dissatisfaction by the Trial Chamber, but given your observations, we certainly will give them strong consideration. And I take it as far as your other remarks go, you are more or less urging the Defence teams to get together before the next hearing to sort of iron out some of these problems to see about -- and I think that's -- with that instruction, I think that our colleague -- my colleagues will certainly meet and discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a break, a 20-minute break. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming our hearing. I will give the floor back to Stojic's Defence so that they can tell us what kind of time you need to put questions to your witnesses. Mr. Khan, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President. Your Honours, dealing with matters in reverse order, the first clarification I can give is that there is no intention on the part of the Stojic Defence to call their client, our client, as a Defence witness. So it's not anticipated that Mr. Stojic will avail himself of the opportunity to give evidence in his own defence. Your Honour, whilst, therefore, the order or the placing of an accused is not relevant to us, it may be of some assistance, I don't -- I'm not sure, just to hopefully shed some light on the exchange that took place between my learned friend Mr. Karnavas and the Bench. Your Honour, the case law from the Tribunal as I understand it, of course, is silent on the order of when an accused will give evidence. I think the practice, as far as I'm aware, has generally been that an accused has given evidence first but different systems have different responses to a question. I do know that the Special Court for Sierra Leone, for example, requires that an accused gives evidence first. And that's the domestic practice in England and Wales. The civil law approach of course is different. I think, Your Honour, that can be matter of course between the Bench and an accused. I think the key point is, hopefully helpful, is that an accused should be given clear notice by the Bench that if he wishes to give evidence at the end or at any point, for example, at the beginning, whether or not it will affect the weight the testimony will give, because there is case law, of course, on that particular issue, and I think if there's no suggestion from the Bench that weight will be viewed prejudicially to an accused depending upon where his counsel seeks to interpose him, I think it's not really an issue that we need to trouble ourselves with. Your Honour, on the core issues it's anticipated that the Stojic Defence will call not more than 30 witnesses, not more than 30 witnesses. And two will be experts. And one of those experts, it's been agreed with the -- all other co-accused teams, will be a common expert that's called in the Stojic defence case. Your Honour, the time that the Defence need will be between 60 to 70 hours in total. Your Honour, there will be one application in relation to one witness -- sorry in relation to two witnesses that they be accorded category B protective status. That will be filed today in compliance with Your Honour's previous instruction. And in relation to one further witness, an application will be filed by the 31st of March that a category A status be accorded to that witness. So out of the 30 witnesses, two will be category B witnesses if our application is granted, and one would be a category A witness. Your Honour, I must address, just to clarify a suggestion put forward by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas. Of course it's hoped that in a perfect world in which the Defence all riding together witnesses could be common to various issues, but it must be said that at this point at least I have not seen, and I think my learned friend has not seen, any summaries, any statements, nor have we been involved in any witness interviews or witness preparation with any witnesses that my learned friend Mr. Karnavas states may well be termed "common witnesses," and at this juncture at least, I think this unilateral declaration of commonality is perhaps premature. I think, Your Honours, with my respectful submission, is that matters will be somewhat clearer once the 65 ter summaries have been served and we can actually make an informed decision in relation to which witnesses are common, which are not, and so I won't say more at this point. Other than it is also anticipated that in the Stojic defence there may well be witnesses subject to the views of counsel for the other co-accused. There may be well be witnesses that maybe of utility to their own cases. Your Honour, that puts me -- brings me one to a further observation by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, and Your Honours hopefully will forgive me if I'm being rather dimwitted about matters, but I must confess I didn't see -- I didn't fully understand the import or the point of the submissions by my learned friend, Mr. Karnavas, about witnesses and evidence in chief and cross-examination. The rules are very clear, and I think sometimes the compartmentalise approach adds to clarity. If, for example, when the 65 ter summaries are given a witness is common, of course in all the summaries it can say this is a common witness. If in a 65 ter summary some witness are on more than one 65 summary list, of course Your Honour knows that witness has been spoken to by more than one Defence team and will be a common witness between at least two particular teams. But, Your Honour, no one can force a witness to be a joint Defence witness. It may well be the case that a witness wishes to give evidence, for example, for Bruno Stojic, whilst he may well or she may well give evidence that may have utility to other accused. Well, that's the purpose of cross-examination. There's no point in forcing a hat on a particular witness against a witness's will. Your Honour, in addition to that, Rule 90 is very clear that cross-examination, and of course, firstly it would ordinarily be limited to examination-in-chief, but, Your Honour, a witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, and there's no rule requiring that leading questions be asked. It's not like examination-in-chief where leading questions on contentious issues are frowned upon and are ordinarily circumscribed. In cross-examination it's completely within the discretion of the cross-examining party to ask completely non-leading questions. So in my respectful submission there's no need for extra, complicated, new, unnecessary rules which don't add, in my view, anything to the practice of the Tribunal. And, Your Honour, I know Mr. President has dealt with many other multi-handed cases. If an accused wishes to elicit evidence from a witness called by another accused he may do so, and he may ask that either by way of leading questions or by way of non-leading questions, the categorisation of the question, of course, is hardly relevant. The evidence that is elicited is. That is the evidence upon which Your Honours, at the end of the case, will determine the guilt and innocence -- the guilt or not of the accused that are sat in the dock today. So, Your Honour, I would urge caution about extra innovation in relation to joint witnesses and the rest of it if that is not explicitly agreed in advance by the Defence teams, and I don't see any prejudice that could possibly arise to any accused in eliciting evidence from a witness called by another party in any form that they seem fit without forcing a label of "joint witness" on a particular witness. Your Honour, I think those are the matters in relation to the item 2 of the agenda that I can respond to at the moment unless Your Honours have any specific question arising from what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, you have a problem with leading questions or suggestive questions. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, when a witness is called by one of the parties, the party in question puts questions to the witness, and the questions are non-leading. That is during examination-in-chief, but the other counsel for the other accused can put leading questions. This is part of the cross-examination. And they can also not put questions, but they're entitled to do so, so I think everybody is agreed on that. So as far as Mr. Stojic is concerned, he will not testify, and you said you would call 30 witnesses approximately, and you will need something ranging from 60 to 70 hours, to sum up what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and not more than 30 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We shall now move on to Mr. Praljak's Defence. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As far as the defence of General Praljak is concerned, with a certain dose of reserve because we're still doing our analyses, and of course from the discussion it is obvious that we'll have to see other lists, too -- or, in other words, let's make a hypothetical here. If we were to set the parameters and framework so that -- the Defence of General Praljak ourselves independently, then I would say to you that we plan, once again roughly speaking, to have 140 to 150 hours for direct, for examination-in-chief, which means about nine -- eight or nine weeks, roughly, working weeks if we have four working days per week as we have worked thus far, and there we include the following: First and foremost, the testimony of General Praljak himself, which would be about -- take about three weeks, four days a week, according to our working schedule so far. So 16 working hours a week or 45 -- about 45 hours for the examination-in-chief. And I don't include in that figure -- or, rather, partially, I partially include, because I don't know what the position of the Prosecution will be, but we have three expert witnesses plus one joint expert witness to be called together with General Petkovic. So these four expert witnesses will be dealing with five different topics in total. I don't know whether the Prosecution will agree or not to the expert testimony, but anyway, this could be about 30 and -- to 40 witnesses under 92 ter, and about 120 to 130 witnesses under 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, and about 20 to 25 witnesses in vivo, with the proviso that and I would like to follow on from what Mr. Karnavas said and inform the Trial Chamber that we have no intention of playing hide and seek, hiding our tactics and so on. I'm telling you of our figures in advance. Of course subject to some more analysis. But what I wish to emphasise is that of the 92 bis and 92 ter witnesses, we would, in a regular trial or -- how shall I put this -- and without the time constraints that we are under, we would very much like to bring in these witnesses for live testimony. Of course we are fully aware of the realistic circumstances, and that is why a lot of witnesses will be heard through the instruments of Rule 92 bis and 92 ter. But I'd like to mention also that when these submissions are submitted, the Defence is absolutely flexible and open, and we don't intend to oppose any comments or objections made by the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber or other Defence teams. That is to say that we should bring in some more witnesses live. We always think that that is a good idea, but in order to be real, realistic, we have to use the 92 ter and 92 bis options. There will be one 92 quater -- or there was to be one, but unfortunately he is deceased. Now, with respect to the testimony of General Praljak himself, I don't want to repeat what's already been said, but my position is this: In conformity with the rules and regulations, which do not specify a time for the testimony of the accused, and in conformity with the cases that have been heard at this Tribunal, although I don't think that there is any jurisprudence in the sense of rulings and decisions, so the Defence does have freedom to plan, and the Trial Chamber will of course have the final word in the matter, but bearing in mind what Judge Antonetti said a moment ago, and we will consider that with all due attention, our original plan is for General Praljak to testify at the beginning, straight away, and that he should open our Defence case from the practical aspect, primarily because through him we could introduce a large number of documents and receive direct comments and have the documents authenticated. And I would like to remind you that General Praljak as opposed to other witnesses knows much more about the facts and therefore can testify about a -- much broader matters than individual witnesses can, because most of them will focus on a set area, time, or subject. So those witnesses will be able to provide us with the segments and images of -- or fragments, whereas Mr. Praljak can incorporate a large number of topics. So that is a more realistic option, and we would like to introduce documents through him. As far as the examination-in-chief is concerned itself, and bearing in mind the practice at the Tribunal thus far, and I'm not sure I understood the Presiding Judge a moment ago when he touched upon this matter, I think that when the accused testifies based on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and he is questioned by the Defence counsel and the Judges of course have the right as they do with any other witness to ask direct questions, and even with less restrictions than you yourselves have introduced as standard practice during the Prosecution case, but again it's quite natural that you might be interested in more things here, more subject matter here. And of course there are limitations and restrictions. And I hope I've understood the Presiding Judge correctly in that respect, that from the moment when the examination-in-chief starts the -- the Defence counsel can no longer have contact with the accused until he completes his testimony. So that is the practical reason for which I think that he should testify straight away. Now, bearing in mind what the Trial Chamber said a moment ago, I see no obstacle that at the end of the Praljak defence the Trial Chamber can ask the accused to appear again to answer some questions from the Bench. I'm not going to enter into that. I just would like to say that that is technically quite possible. It is feasible. If I were to conduct my defence case in an ideal manner as I see fit, under ideal circumstances, I think the method of presentation is important, how to paint the picture you wish to paint. And therefore I would choose to start off with General Praljak and his testimony, and then continue looking into the different areas, events, topics and other exhibits. Of course, with 92 ter witnesses thrown in. So when I have enough grounds and a good base, and the Defence teams before me will do that, then we can go ahead with 92 bis witnesses as well. But I'm quite sure that you know from what has been said thus far that in the meantime we'll look at other lists and see where we can add something to the others or take some away. Now, I've been told by my colleague that I wasn't quite clear because I failed to state that as far as we can see now, we're going to have approximately 20, perhaps a little more, viva voce witnesses. As I say, a little more than 20 viva voce witnesses. I did say it. Right. Then I apologise. Perhaps it wasn't correctly transcribed in the record. I don't want to take up too much of our time, so if you have any questions to ask, please feel free to do so, but I think I've tackled them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was listening to you, I discovered something which I hadn't thought of until now, and I don't know if we've ever had such a case. Your client, Mr. Praljak, is going to testify, which means that he will be sitting over there in front of us. He will take the solemn declaration, and you will put questions to him. Normally speaking these should be non-leading questions. So you will ask him questions. And you have told us that you had planned three weeks for this. Since you need 45 hours, that all in all will amount to three weeks. And then you added something, and I think this is something quite new. You said will you then not be able to have any contact with him if he takes the solemn declaration? He then is a witness of the Chamber, or can he then continue talking to you during and after his testimony, and I don't have an answer to that question. This is something which I never had -- which had never occurred to me. I think we need to discuss this. The Bench needs to look into the matter. This is something quite new. I don't know what happened in the other cases, but since you are his counsel, I don't see how one could prevent a counsel from talking to his client. That is an answer to the question. But the Trial Chamber has into the deliberated on the matter yet. To me it seems quite clear that an accused who is testifying is answering questions put by his counsel or her counsel, but these questions are non-leading questions. I think everybody agrees on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is how I view the matter: As far as leading questions, I think there's no dilemma there. When the accused is testifying, he is testifying the same way as any other witness would. He is in the position of a witness. And when the Defence counsel asks questions, they're not leading ones. I don't -- they shouldn't be leading ones. There is no dilemma there. Now when I said restricted or limited contact between the client and the Defence counsel, so while the client is testifying he is a witness. Now, I said that for two reasons. The first is that I as Defence counsel and case manager as well, try to plan the worst case scenario as far as I'm concerned, whether there will be any restrictions or limitations placed upon me. Secondly, this restriction was specifically raised in the earlier trial, Kordic and Cerkez, where we had planned to have our client testify, but unfortunately for some other reasons we weren't able to call him. And then the Presiding Judge said, as an instructions, that while the accused is testifying Defence counsel cannot have contacts with him as a Defence counsel, and I think that emanates from British law, British legal practice. Perhaps Mr. Khan could help us out here. But since the accused has two counsels, then the other counsel, Defence counsel, can deal with procedural issues that might arise, or cannot. So I am going to -- I want to be prepared for a full scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, can you enlighten us, please, as regards this law which seems to be specifically British?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, its origins, of course, are common -- are general in the common law system, but it is the practice in this Tribunal that once any witness, and when a witness is in the dock, whether it's an accused or not, there's no special rule they're all witnesses of the Trial Chamber. And when a Prosecution witness takes the oath, the Prosecution are prohibited from speaking to that witness once the evidence is completed. Of course once that witness has been cross-examined or has been re-examined, Your Honour, contact in the usual way can take place, the witness can be thanked, and the same would apply to a Defence counsel. Your Honour, what happens in domestic systems on occasion, is that during -- once an accused takes the dock, there may be some emergency, something, personal matter, something crops up, and, Your Honour, what happens then is that the counsel stands up and makes a submission to the Court to speak to an accused on a particular issue. For example, God forbid, if there's a family bereavement or there is some other matter, one gets leave of the Trial Chamber to speak to a witness on a particular issue. But, Your Honour, it's founded in good sense of course because it's to present any party on any side making allegations of coaching, that the evidence has been molded as it goes along and damages being repaired, and that's where the rule comes from. And I think as matter of equity, of course, we wish Defence witnesses to be treated under the same conditions as the Prosecution witnesses. We put them forward as witnesses of truth. Speaking for the Stojic case, and we would ask that nothing be done that could undermine the weight that would be afforded to these witnesses at the end of the day. Your Honour, I don't know if that assists at all but that's the background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, I've listened to you and you've told us quite clearly how this works in the British system, but we are in a particular system here. If Mr. Praljak testifies first before the witnesses that you intend to call and then the counsel can no longer contact him, how will the Defence counsel continue to prepare the future witnesses, the interviews, if he has no contact with his client? He can get no instructions from his client anymore. Let's assume a particular case, for instance, in which months later another witness is called and the Defence counsel needs to know how he has to put his questions, what the issue focuses on. And if he can't discuss a matter with his client, he may run into real difficulties. How do you settle that issue in your system?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I have been unclear. The rule only applies as long as the witness sits in the dock -- sits in the witness box. Once his evidence is completed, for example, if he's the first witness, once the evidence is completed and re-examination is finished, of course normal contact, normal business resumes in the usual manner. There's no prohibition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but if, for instance, he is sitting in the witness box for three weeks and he is there for three weeks, this means that for three weeks the counsel cannot discuss anything with him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, without the leave of the Court, and that's to ensure the integrity of the evidence that Your Honours hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think that this has been made quite clear. Thank you, Mr. Khan, not addressing you, and I think it's also perfectly convincing. I have a question to Mr. Kovacic. I have a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel has said that this is convincing, but it's not convincing as far as I'm concerned, because I don't see why a counsel cannot talk to his client. I must say I'm flabbergasted. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kahn has made that clear. There is a suspicion. If you have your client on the dock as a witness is during the day, in the evening you go in a meeting with him, the suspicion will be that you say, "You did very well on that point. On that point tomorrow I will ask you so that you can change and clarify and don't touch upon that when I ask you. Do not give that answer," and so forth. And then the evidence of the accused, as witness, is devaluated, and that is to be avoided. So I seem to understand and approve of that system. But I wanted to raise another point. I think I do not -- do you want to embark on a quite different answer or just confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
