utterances.text: I wanted to say something on this topic but something that hadn't already been said because if it had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I want to say was that Mr. Khan has covered as far as I'm concerned everything British. And I'm with him on everything British that he has said. Everything to do with England and Wales law and procedure, from Mr. Kahn, I adopt from today and probably forever, actually, because he's nearly always right, but what I wanted to say was that it's entirely consistent and endorsed by the practice in this Tribunal. I've been in a previous trial where my client gave evidence and the arrangement was in practice exactly as Mr. Khan describes, that in the course of many weeks of evidence, because I think we should bear in mind that any accused giving evidence in relation to his or her case before this Tribunal is bound to be in the witness box for weeks in any case of any complexity because otherwise it simply cannot do their case justice by their evidence. It's bound to be weeks from time to time there was, as there nearly always would be, some practical need to discuss something; it might have been to do with money, it might have been to do with just practical organisation, some need to have some contact with the client, it was never a problem because the Prosecution team being a professional team and recognising the Defence teams as professional teams were always willing to agree and then the Trial Chamber gave its endorsement to do exactly what Mr. Khan describes, a meeting with the accused which you would give in outline the topics that you wanted to discuss that wouldn't be anything to do with the case. And actually, may I add to the general acceptance of the prescription on meeting one's client, apart from in those areas meeting one's client to discuss anything to do with the case during his evidence, that actually we don't want to because we want our client's evidence to be untainted by any possibility that it's been discussed; and also, and I mean no disrespect to my client or anybody else's client, you don't want to because it's humanly impossible to keep off the topic. If you had a complete freedom to discuss anything you like with your client if you met him during his evidence, it wouldn't matter how much you would say to each other, "Oh, no, no we can't discuss your evidence," because if you discuss anything to do with the case at all it's going to have some bearing on his evidence. So the rule and with respect to Mr. President, Your Honour, this rule which is part of English law and practice, also very much the practice before this Tribunal, has fundamental sense to it and it is a rule and Your Honours are I think beginning to see. I can't speak for every Defence counsel. Everybody speaks for themselves, but it's apparent from what Your Honours have been hearing so far that this rule and this practice is whole-heartedly accepted and adopted by the Defence teams in this case, and I'm pretty sure it would be whole-heartedly adopted and endorsed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually, I wanted to raise a different point with Mr. Karnavas. You have -- with Mr. Kovacic. Excuse me. A slip of my tongue. You have indicated that you would need 140 to 150 hours. You have translated that into eight to nine weeks. In fact, Mr. Kovacic, experience shows that if you want to examine in direct for 150 hours, it will take about 30 weeks, because on average our experience so far has shown that not more than one-third, and even less than one-third of the time used is actually effective as direct, and the rest is taken by cross, and there will be -- there may be complicated cross-examination by your colleagues of the Defence team and by the Prosecutor. And you may not like it and it may sometimes perhaps be critical, but the Judges take an active interest in the case and they also ask questions, plus procedural issues arise. So I wonder whether you were aware of the fact that we are talking about more than half a year.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, unfortunately, yes, I was aware of that fact. We are constantly trying to simulate the time we need. It's become one of our favourite topics of conversation. I'm not a good mathematician, but I've become very quick in computing hours of witness examination and relating it to the calendar, but with all due respect for the completion strategy of the UN, it was not I who drafted the indictment. It was the OTP. And as you know, accoladis graecus, the Defence has tried to convince the OTP that this doesn't make sense even in the pre-trial period, the maxim of concentration also goes against it, but the OTP insisted on the indictment as it now stands and the accused have the right to defend themselves. Your Honours will hand down a decision as to the allocation of time, and you will be hard pressed to reach your decision. If I were alone in this case, if there were not six accused but one, and if there was no completion strategy, I would be asking for far more time, but as Your Honours know, one viva voce testimony is worth far more than any amount of statements on paper. So although 92 bis and other witnesses I intend to call will not be as valuable as the viva voce witnesses. I seem to have prompted this discussion with an aside, but I mentioned the relation between counsel and accused during the trial because as Judge Antonetti once said, the lead counsel is also the case manager, and the length of testimony of the accused is an aspect I have to bear in mind, and now we're all aware of these points. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Let's assume for the sake of argument -- but a Judge of course, worth his salt, has to envision all types of situation. Let's assume that an accused person takes the stand and that his statements challenge the case as prepared by his counsel. What should a Defence counsel do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to admit you've caught me unawares. I did not anticipate your question. May I have just a moment, please. My colleague is reminding me of an important point which I have to raise right away in spite of the fact that you've caught me unawares. In our particular case, as in every case, the accused and the Defence counsel prepare the defence strategy together. There is no doubt about that. My ethics as a lawyer does not permit me to prepare any kind of defence case or strategy without the agreement of my client. It may or may not be my idea, but the client has to accept it. The client can also suggest a strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what about if your client suddenly changes course with respect to your strategy? What happens then? What does the counsel do, because counsel is not in a position to have any contact with his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- well, these are now profound ethical issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I take the floor, and I would like to say without any attempt to take our time and your time on that issue, as far as the client and the Defence lawyer's relationship, I do believe that here is a very clear-cut right for the -- for those -- I mean this accused to be a witness as well. On the other hand, let me emphasise that it is on the very risk of the accused if he takes the stand and if he takes the dock and he will go there, so it is up to him himself and up to the lawyer, his lawyer, of course, to make this decision if the accused would like to appear independently as a witness. So therefore I do not see here too much problem. The witness should -- if he takes the stand as a witness, then he should accept the responsibility for it. And therefore, if anything happens, then of course it is up to the detriment of the accused and the detriment of the lawyer as well. They have to face the situation that whenever they will take this step they are going to be in a way in the hands of the Chamber, of course, and according to the rules. And therefore, evidently, I do not think that we have to be afraid of the situation. Then we will see what will happen if, let's say, one of the accused will take the dock for three weeks, and he cannot speak to his lawyer during that very time, then it is up to him to face the consequences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour. I agree fully with the standpoint of Judge Prandler. Of course, needless to say, this Defence, in consultation with a client, considered all the pros and cons, all the advantages and disadvantages. This of course is normal. What confuses me a little bit in the question put by His Honour, the Presiding Judge, is what if the client suddenly changes his strategy in the course of his testimony. That part I find a little bit confusing because it touches on profound ethical issues. I think that the ethical guidelines every counsel has to abide by provides guidance in this respect. If the client changes strategy, it's the duty of the Defence counsel to warn the client of the consequences of his actions. That would be the first step. If, however, there is such a deep-seeded and profound conflict that it threatens the Defence case, and if the Defence counsel for ethical reasons cannot or must not agree with the client's strategy, then of course his power of attorney should be terminated. He should no longer appear for the client. But these are all very profound issues, and I think that here we must all be bound by the ethical rules of our bar association, not only our national bar association but also the Association of Defence Counsel before this Tribunal if such a conflict develops. Then of course it has to be resolved accordingly. However, my colleague has told me that I may have omitted in my assessment of the hours needed, 140 to 150, I may have omitted to say that this would include the testimony of General Praljak. We also believe, looking at the trends in the OTP case, that the relationship between the time needed for the examination-in-chief and the time needed for cross-examination and Judges' question -- questions has improved considerably. Initially we wasted much more time on procedural issues, and this improved as the trial went on. So we do not think that much time will be wasted during the Defence case of General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be very brief. I'm 63 years old. I'm mentally fit. I'm still reasonable. I have no psychological problems, and my health is good. I'm aware that I want to testify. I wish to thank you for your warning that this might be to my detriment, but I'm not afraid of that. My strategy and the strategy of my counsel is very simple. It is to under oath tell the truth about the events that took place, the time when they took place, the development of the situation as I saw it, to present all the documents, all my explanations as a general and a soldier who was there, also as a professor of sociology, matters concerning electrical engineering, water supply, and so on and so forth. I intend to state clearly without any fear all these things regardless of whatever consequences this may have on my future life. I am not afraid of any decision Your Honours may hand down, hoping that you will view every issue from all aspects. I am prepared to abide by everything I say. I can distinguish between what is my own personal experience, what I learned about in other ways, and I can explain how the situation developed in that area at that time, primarily from my point of view, which was very broad. And speaking quite frankly, I have been preparing for almost a decade, so I do not need to consult my lawyer in the meantime during my testimony, because this will be a precise scenario with precise segments as to what I will talk about, what documents will illustrate and support my answers, and also which of the 200 witnesses or so who made their statements -- gave their statements and had them verified by a court can support this, and then you can call on those witnesses to check whether everything I have said is the truth. I don't want to dabble in legal matters, but my Defence strategy is to speak clearly and precisely regardless of any consequences this may have for myself, and I'm not afraid of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Kovacic, 100 to 150 hours through 30 to 40, 92 ter witnesses, one 92 quater witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed one number of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of documents, do you have any idea about the number of documents you'll produce through these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point, to be quite frank, we have on our list approximately 3.500 documents. However, don't take fright, please. We're working on sifting through this list, and we're looking to see whether something has been duplicated in part or in total, whether a document has already been admitted into evidence and so on. So we're going through it again to see whether we actually do need all these documents, and where we can cut documents from four down to two we shall do that. So we adopted various criteria and put on the list everything we thought we needed. That was the first stage, and now we're sifting through it. That's stage two. But Mr. Praljak would like to say something. But before you give him the floor, I'd like to say something else. Perhaps this is what General Praljak wished to bring too. If we take certain topics, I want to anticipate certain things. Certain topics that I refer to a contrario topics with respect to the joint criminal enterprise and its existence, for example, why Croatia, the state of Croatia, offered permanent ongoing and extensive assistance, for example, in the area of healthcare, and why it treated in its hospitals not only Croats and Muslims, civilians, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also Croats and Muslims who were soldiers. They were treated in Croatian hospitals as well. You have heard evidence about that, a little evidence. Now, we had to ask the state and these hospitals to provide us with the necessary documents. We received thousands of them, thousands in response to our request. So quite obviously as there's no sense in or practical possibilities of providing you with all those several thousand documents. So to cut a long story short, we chose certain documents that were indicative, letters from the ministry providing information and so on and so forth. So as I say, all the DVD material provided electronically, we'll disclose it to the opposite side and then they can go through them and say, "That is not correct," for example. We're going to give you the top of the iceberg during our case, and if anybody has any doubts, then they can go back to all those documents and raise their questions. So there are several topics like that and for the purposes of illustration perhaps it would be a good idea for General Praljak to tell you more about it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just with respect to the assistance given by Croatia in taking in refugees, armaments, education, and so on, there are more than 8.000 documents in 96 binders which are here in The Hague. Now, the problem of taking in refugees in Posusje, we have over 8.000 documents there. The problem of humanitarian assistance in Mostar, we have thousands of documents on that. With respect to the flats of Muslims remaining in Mostar, we have thousands of documents on that too. So the number of documents that my team could submit surpasses 50.000. There are 19 binders, 96 binders, 8 binders on all these different topics. So the figures quoted by my counsel Mr. Kovacic of 3.500, that is the minimum number of documents. Of course there are summaries, pre-cease and so on, but number of documents that this Trial Chamber could look at, they will be on CDs and they will be summaries with charts and tables, everything will be accessible so it can be tested and verified. So as I say there are over 50.000 documents which exist in our database which could provide assistance to the Trial Chamber to gain a picture of what was relevant and what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to D4. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'll be pretty brief. I don't want to give the impression that Mr. Khan and I and Mr. Sahota have underneath our robes some England shirt with three lions on it, but I do once again agree with Mr. Khan's approach and everything that he has said. And particularly, I can summarise, he was saying Please, can we keep it simple. Please can we keep it as simple as possible. And that's very much an approach which we the Petkovic Defence will endorse. An illustration of that, by the way Your Honour, I'm not sure quite sure how material it is right now, but the question that Your Honour posed, what happens when your client gives some evidence which inconsistent with the case as you have understood it. Your Honour, it's a difficult situation. It is one that is often faced by counsel. It's not a difficult question in the end, Your Honour. The answer to that is your client comes up with something unexpected in evidence, you -- you swear under your breath. You count to ten. You know that the principle is that you have to adapt the way you present the case to the evidence your client is giving rather than the other way round. If the client's mistaken or got confused, of course it's your job to correct that and make sure he doesn't do himself injustice, but his evidence is his evidence and you just have to adapt. And that's in the end -- actually is isn't that difficult. It's not some profound issue, it's a good example, and with respect to Mr. Kovacic, it's a good example as if one bears the basic principles in mind, keeps one's eye on the ball, it provides an easy solution to a difficult situation, but one that does happen from time to time. But, Your Honour in endorsing as I do the approach set up by Mr. Khan and therefore not repeating it or not needing really to add to it, I just confine myself to this: First of all we understand the purpose of this preliminary hearing is for us to give Your Honours as much help as we reasonably can at the moment and give as much steer as we reasonably can as to where we're going given that we haven't got to the 31st of March, we haven't completed that exercise. Your Honours haven't got the 65 ter lists. The final decisions on these things have to be taken at a later point. But in a spirit of helpfulness of course we will offer this. We will say for the Petkovic Defence, Your Honour, that we will have no more than 30 witnesses, and we hope it's helpful for you to know that. We will have, as Mr. Kovacic has already indicated, we will have one, an expert witness in common or shared with General Praljak, and that's a military expert. We plan to have one other witness on constitutional matters which we expect will be shared with possibly not every accused because after all it doesn't have to be all or nothing. It's quite possible that we will share with one or two or whatever, but that's open. The estimate at the -- well, I should say the next point is that it is undecided and may remain undecided for some considerable time which is our right as to whether Petkovic himself will give evidence. Without his evidence, Your Honour, our estimate is that the -- our witnesses will require I say not more than 80 hours. That's not terribly different from the time put forward by Mr. Khan for his client, or Mr. Stojic, but we say not more than 80 hours. But again I hope that Your Honour will accept that on all this it's slightly early days, although we're getting close to when the Defence case has to come up, it's still slightly early days so far as refining these figures are concerned, and it also follows from the numbers that I have given Your Honour that the question of 92 ter, and 92 bis and so on, it's a far less significance and impact as it is in the light of -- in Mr. -- in General Praljak's case given the very large number of potential witnesses and potential 92 bis, 92 ter witnesses that have been suggested by Mr. Kovacic is on a different scale as far as that's concerned, so we don't need to get into it. The -- so far as -- I will offer just a couple of comments on the question of when an accused should give evidence if he is called to give evidence. Certainly the -- the norm as far as we are concerned is that he would give evidence first. What we do say, Your Honour, is that it should primarily be a matter for the Defence's choice as to when their client gives evidence, but it also observe this, that there are reasons for the practice of a Defence -- of an accused normally giving evidence first and they've been touched on. And if it is to be later in the case and if the Defence needs to be confident that nobody is going to suggest that any adverse influence should be drawn and any adverse light cast upon the evidence of an accused because he doesn't give evidence first, that first all requires in effect a commitment in advance which is difficult, Your Honour, a commitment in advance from the Trial Chamber that not having yet heard the evidence they will not assess it adversely in any way, but it also effectively requires a commitment from the Prosecution and they may find that difficult to do. They may find it very difficult to say that before they've her the evidence of the accused and before they've heard the evidence of any other witnesses, they're going to give up any right to suggest that the evidence given is in some way diminished or devalued by the fact that somebody has already heard somebody else's evidence, somebody -- the evidence is going to be dealt with in a particular order. So, Your Honour, it's -- it's fraught with difficulties and again we urge to keep that as simple as possible, but in principle it should be primarily a matter for -- well, certainly it's a matter for Defence with all the warnings we're helpfully reminded of by His Honour Judge Prandler. It's a matter for the Defence as to whether the accused gives evidence at all, but then if he does a matter primarily for the Defence as to when it's done. But, Your Honour, unless there is anything we can immediately help Your Honours with, those are our preliminary, and hope helpful indications, as to where we are going so far as the presentation of the Petkovic Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. When it comes to D4, you're talking about 80 hours, 30 witnesses, one military expert witness, one witness constitutional law. With respect to Mr. Petkovic, you have not yet decided whether he's going to testify or not. Let me ask a question. As for the military expert witness, can you give us his name if you know it already?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Koriance [Pronounced phonetically] is the way I'm saying it. Milan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to say good afternoon to you all. It is a military expert. He will be a joint witness together with the Praljak Defence. The gentleman's name is Milan, Gorjanc. He is a citizen, a national of the Republic of Slovenia. He was a highly positioned officer in the Yugoslav People's Army and knows about the events in the former Yugoslavia very well, and I think he will be of great importance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I first must say if it prevents some poor unsuspecting gentlemen in the heart of England being identified as an expert witness in a case he's never heard of. Your Honours, I just want to make it absolutely clear if it wasn't crystal clear that the 80 hours is without General Petkovic. So that if General Petkovic does give evidence what I said earlier applies clearly without estimating in detail how long clearly as with any accused in this case that's -- that must be -- that must be weeks because of the sheer complexity of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might be allowed to make a correction. On page 60, line 17, you summarised and stated figures. I heard you correctly, but this isn't reflected in the transcript. The numbers are as follows: About 150 hours total, including General Praljak, and between 30 to 40, 92 ter witnesses. That's correct. And then between 120 to 130 92 bis witnesses just for the record. I heard you say it correctly but I feel that the transcript does not record that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. D5 now, Mr. Coric's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. Your Honour, I'm sorry to intervene, but if I may just ask, for the purposes of the record, the name Milan Goriance, was that the correct spelling of Goriance, G-O-R-I-A-N-C-E? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That isn't the correct spelling of the surname. I'm going to spell it letter by letter. G as in Greece, O as Opatija, R as Romania, J as in Japan, A as in Austria, N as in Netherlands, and C as in Cyprus. Gorjanc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For Mr. Coric now. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence of Mr. Coric when it drew up its plan of the Defence case it wanted to have and reasonable number of witnesses, and at this point in time what I can tell you is this: We're going to have about 25 witnesses, of which just a few of them will be 92 ter witnesses. We haven't made the decision as to exactly how many. But if everything goes according to plan, we're not going to have any 92 bis or 92 quater witnesses. Of the 25 witnesses one is an expert witness, and now apart from those witnesses we're going to have one joint expert witness, and all the Defence teams I think agreed several months ago it is an expert in constitutional matters. However, I don't count him within our time. I'd just like to tell you that there is this joint witness. That is the joint agreement that I have been privy to thus far. Mr. Coric will be testifying himself, and it is our plan precisely for the reasons presented by Judge Antonetti that he should testify at the end of the Defence case. As for those 25 witnesses that we plan to call, we think we'll need about 50 hours to get through them. And for Mr. Coric's testimony 20 hours. That makes it a total of 70 hours. And I also wanted to state with relation to the matter of contacts with the accused during his testimony, when I first heard that there was the possibility of banning the Defence counsel from contacting with his client during testimony, I reacted, I must say, in the same way as the Presiding Judge, and I'm troubled by the same dilemma still. However, as far as I've been informed, in the Milutinovic trial there was one accused who took the floor, and the principle was the same. It was applied. That is to say while he was in the witness chair, his Defence counsel could not have any contact with him. That's as far as I know. I'd just like to say with respect to the joint witnesses mentioned by Mr. Karnavas a moment ago that I as yet don't know which witnesses will be the ones called by Mr. Karnavas and what they're going to talk about, but I believe Mr. Karnavas when he says that they are witnesses who are going to speak about topics of joint interest, but at this point in time I have no additional information, nothing more than that, apart from what I've heard in the courtroom this afternoon. So I can't state whether they will actually be joint witnesses or not. That's what I wanted to say with respect to the Coric Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much you were very clear. Seventy hours, out of which 20 for Mr. Coric and 50 for your 25 witnesses. Fine. Now D6, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no dilemmas when to call the accused at the beginning or at the end. Mr. Pusic, and I'd like to say for the record, will not be testifying to his advantage in this trial. Now, when this comes to other matters, we are modest in terms of time, and we envisage a maximum of approximately 30 hours with 12 to 15 witnesses to be called. Now, this number of ours will probably be less than the 30 hours. Some witnesses will be testifying under 92 bis or 92 ter, which will dramatically, of course, reduce the number of hours we need for our defence case. Of course we're going to attend the proceedings with all due attention, and we reserve the right to amend the witness list, with the permission from the Trial Chamber of course, and once again within the number of hours that we have asked for, and we will not overstep the limit and your rulings about time. I don't exclude the possibility that the Pusic Defence stands up and says that it's going to close the case and not mount a Defence case, not call any witnesses at all. So that is another possibility which we will decide upon subsequently. So those of our forecasts. A maximum of about 30 hours with every possibility of needing fewer hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So I've done my sums, and so we have some 570 or 75 hours if we add up the upper bracket of your estimates. The Prosecution had under 300 hours, as a reminder. So this is the problem as it now stands. Of course the Trial Judges will convene and discuss all this, but of course only when we have the summaries will we see things more clearly. Indeed, for the time being there's nothing we can add to this, but this is a figure that will be food for thought for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Without attempting to preempt the decision of the Chamber on those issues which we have discussed so far, I would only like to draw your attention along the lines what our president just said, that I would like to ask you, I mean the Defence teams, to study the memorandum which was prepared by the greffier, by Mr. Chuka, who is here actually, and it was issued dated February the 5th, 2008, and it is about the time monitoring, the period ending 24 January, and here we will see, and we will see and you will see that the total sitting hours have been 984, which roughly is about 1.000 hours. Out of the 1.000 hours, the OTP, the Prosecution, took 30 per cent, 3-0, for the direct examination and the examination, and the Defence, as far as the total cross-examination is concerned, took 37 per cent, that time which amounted to 364 hours. Now, I'm not going into the details, that is the how many hours this or that Defence took, but now in comparison with the present figures which we have heard and the Presiding Judge Antonetti has already mentioned this, it amounts altogether the wishes and the submissions by the Defence teams that altogether 570, which almost twice as much as what the OTP took by presenting its case, i.e., that they took, as it was mentioned, 296 hours versus 570 hours as now requested. So -- and I'm sorry, I should also mention that the -- that actually the procedural matters took 22 per cent of the time, and the questions by Judges - excuse me - took 11 per cent. That is 22 for procedural matters, 11 for the Judges' questions. I believe that we all -- we have to study carefully all these figures, both which is actually for the total sitting hours so far and also as envisaged as planned by the Defence. So then the Trial Chamber should take into account those issues which I have just mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, if I may just very briefly comment on three aspects. The first aspect, and that is probably the most important from the point of view of the Prosecution, is exactly what Your Honour, Mr. President, you, and what Judge Prandler have now pointed out, and that is that the Prosecution used, and we can round it up to 300 hours, for the presentation of its case. That was already much reduced time from what the Prosecution originally requested. Based on that, Your Honour, the point that the Prosecution would make is that it would be very unfair if the Defence were granted unlimited time to refute the Prosecution case if the Prosecution was forced to -- or -- not forced, but if the time allocated to the Prosecution was limited. That is the first point, Your Honour, and in line with that the basic stand of the Prosecution would be that 300 hours for the Defence overall would be a useful guideline to depart from and to work around that figure. Your Honour, the two other points that the Prosecution would raise, the first pertains to a suggestion made by Mr. Karnavas, my learned friend, and that pertains to the aspect of a witness being called by one party and then another accused or Defence wishing to also ask questions in direct examination or solicit direct evidence from that witness. The suggestion made by Mr. Karnavas that such Defence would have to notify or at least request certain time for direct examination. It does appeal to the Prosecution and for the following reason, that there was some concern on the side of the Prosecution that a witness may be called by one defendant but during cross-examination by other defendants they may solicit direct evidence under the guise of cross-examination. In other words, asking very easy, direct questions and soliciting evidence by way of leading questions, which may pose some problems. If I may just mention regarding that, I do recall that we have had this discussion previously and that Judge Trechsel did identify certain jurisprudence or legal principles stating that under direct or cross-examination there is the situation that leading questions would be permitted where new evidence or direct evidence is being solicited. But I leave that at this stage. I won't belabour the point. The second point refers to the discussion we had regarding the status of an accused testifying and the position that his Defence counsel would find themselves in, whether they may contact the accused or not, and with regard to that I wish to say that my learned colleague Mr. Stewart was actually correct when he said that -- or suggested that the Prosecution would agree with the Prosecution that he took and with his elaboration of Mr. Khan's setting out of the position. The Prosecution indeed agrees with that and can live with the situation as sketched by them, and then also with the implications as stated by Judge Prandler. Thank you, Your Honour. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, very briefly, Your Honour. I just wanted to supplement that we have approximately 2.000 documents. That was something I omitted to mention and my colleague, Ms. Tomanovic, following the proceedings, reminded me that I was not diligent in making the Trial Chamber aware. With respect to an issue that was brought up by Mr. Khan, nobody's trying to force labels on anybody, but there are witnesses that have, as he put it, might have information that is of utility, and it was on that point, perhaps it was my inarticulate way of phrasing it, saying that where a witness has information that is of value, I don't care who the witness is called by, we would want to be able to elicit testimony from that witness, and sometimes it definitely will be outside the scope of direct examination. In fact, the utility might be of such nature and to such a degree that may be far lengthier than the direct examination that is the purpose for which that particular witness was called upon. In those instances we definitely would like the Trial Chamber to be rather flexible. It matters not to me whether I cross-examine a witness or do direct examination, because in this Tribunal even under -- when you cross you tend to ask non-leading questions, and I think it benefits everyone when that can be done. My primary concern is allocation of time. That's the primary concern. And so if the information is relevant and assists the Trial Chamber, I don't want to be pigeonholed. Cross-examination of a Prosecution witness is very different than -- at this stage of the game. And so while some witnesses are being called by one particular party for whatever reason but have information that assists the Trial Chamber and goes to other cases, then in those instances we would be making or seeking leave for significant time or the time necessary for the purposes of eliciting information. And of course this would be no surprise that many of us are in the field, actually in the field meeting with witnesses, and we know that some of them are -- have committed to be called for one particular party for whatever reason. That doesn't mean that they're not -- nonetheless they are willing to speak to us. Of course you can never force a witness to speak to you in the field, and they're willing to be questioned on the stand. And I leave it for others to decide whether somebody is a witness for X or witness for V. We're not trying to force any labels, and again if I misspoke or was inarticulate in putting my case forward, I apologise, but anyway, I think the point was made. Lastly, the 300 hours, I know that -- that the Prosecution has to start somewhere and I feel like I'm in a middle eastern bazaar now when we start saying, Okay, well they got 300 we should get 300. Well, you know, we've tried to make approximations based on our realistic assessments. Keeping in mind that normally, at least my experience has been, that as you begin to elicit testimony witnesses do tend to drop. Some points are covered through other witnesses. And of course this is our first meeting. We haven't all met to go over our lists respectively, so I suspect that we're going to have a slightly lesser, you know, amount of hours to present to the Trial Chamber as a whole, but I would -- I would urge the Trial Chamber at this point of the proceedings, at this stage, not to set a time limitation keeping in mind that we do recognise that 300 hours were used by the Prosecution. But having said that, it has been my experience on many occasions where I put a two- or three-time lengthier case than the Prosecution case. So there's no fixed rule. Sometimes I put on no case. So I would urge the Trial Chamber to -- and I don't mean to be harsh, but to essentially disregard the comment about limiting us to 300 hours. I mean, with all due respect to my colleague here, I don't think 300 hours is realistic for six individuals, keeping in mind that perhaps 40 per cent of the -- of this trial, if not 60 per cent goes to the -- to the common issue of joint criminal enterprise. And as far as I'm concerned, and I'll be very frank, it matters not command responsibility. Joint criminal enterprise is what the essence of this trial is all about. The rest of it is -- is secondary as far as I'm concerned, and that's why a significant amount of time must be given in addition to what would be allocated to the teams on an individual basis for the common defence. And it doesn't matter who brings the witnesses, the fact of the matter is that there are certain issues that are tangled into this joint criminal enterprise, which in my humble opinion is not even part of customary international law but it's been adopted and concocted by this Tribunal, but nonetheless we're here. We have to fight it. We have to defend against it, and so I would urge that when we look at this you considered that in mind, that 40 to 60 per cent of the case deals with this common issue called joint criminal enterprise, and it touches --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak closer into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- each and every one of the accused because of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may make a very brief observation, very brief. The OTP says that the Defence should have about 300 hours, which is the total amount of time the OTP had. Let me just refer to Rule 82 concerning joint trials which state clearly: [In English] "Each accused shall be accorded the same rights as if such accused." [Interpretation] So I think each one of us would have the right to ask for 300 hours. Of course we are realistic. We know about the exit policy. We are aware of everything my colleague Mr. Karnavas mentioned. We wish to be relevant and realistic, and of course that number will be greatly reduced. But I certainly do not agree that the Prosecution case should be put on the same footing as the total Defence case, because each accused is not one-sixth of the Defence case. Each one has the right to his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break in a few seconds. Rule 82 was mentioned. Don't forget Rule 73 ter either, which makes it obligatory for the Trial Chamber, on the one hand, to assess the number of witnesses, but the Trial Chamber can also, to shorten -- has the possibility of shortening the examination-in-chief of some witnesses. This is 73 ter (B). And the Trial Chamber also has to assess the length. That is Rule 73 ter (E). Having to do so, the Trial Chamber will have to specify the number of hours given to the Defence. There is no other way around. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just make a single comment on that, Your Honour. It cannot possibly be that anything that the Trial Chamber does under Rule 73 ter can compromise or cut across or in any way infringe the rights under Article 82, Rule 82, or indeed any other rights. The hierarchy is absolutely plain. There are all other sorts of rights apart from Rule 82, but so far as there are rights in Rule 82, 73 ter has got to be applied consistently with and supportive of those rights and can't compromise or reduce them in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to make one point. This is in fact a very difficult issue. If you amongst yourselves have talked about, so have we quite a lot. And I think we are all aware that it's a difficult decision. We are not going to take any such decision now, but we will wait until we see what the Defence actually propose, and we will, of course, utilise our power to scrutinise what we think is really germane to the issues before the Chamber and eliminate elements which we think they may be of some interest, but they will not assist us in coming to a result. And for the time being, I think we do not need to go on discussing it. The issue is clearly on the table, and be assured that we will give very careful consideration. The principle just stated by Mr. Stewart, I fully approve. Of course we have to take into account all the guarantees set out in Article 21 of the Statute. That is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one sentence, a piece of calculation which I think will be of interest to everyone? We all know that the witnesses in the Prosecution case were very important for us to present documentary evidence and to try to explain to Your Honours some points. In this way, the OTP introduced 2.200 exhibits. In 18.000 minutes that is 300 hours. They tendered 2.200 exhibits, which means one exhibit per eight minutes. If the same time were awarded to Mr. Prlic's Defence, which wishes to tender 2.000 exhibits, we would need 250 hours for the Defence of Mr. Prlic alone to tender our documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a 20-minute break. We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall resume our work and address item 3, time allocation for cross-examination of Defence witnesses. Now, as far as the Prosecution is concerned and as far as the other accused are concerned. We have 50 minutes left. We won't be able to address all the item on the agenda, so those that we are not able to address today will be addressed at the next Status Conference. As far as item 3 is concerned, this is what the Bench has to say: When a Defence counsel calls one of his or her witnesses, how much time will the other Defence counsel have, and how much time will the Prosecution have? If, for instance, Mr. Petkovic calls a witness for two hours and his cross-examination therefore will last two hours, how much time will the other Defence counsel have to cross-examine this witness, and how much time will the Prosecution have for this same witness. So this is a question which we would like to address, and we shall listen to what you have of to say about it, and the Bench will decide on the basis of what you have to say. The Prosecution, of course, will take the floor on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just two points. The first is that of course now it is practically impossible to tell because you do not have the list of the witnesses. You do not know what they're going to testify about. So it would be sheer guesswork, I think. Second, I could imagine an instrument where you have a list of all the witnesses, then the time used for direct, and then open columns in which each team, Defence team and the Prosecution, would enter the time they anticipate they need. That might be very useful for the organisation of the Chamber's work but also for -- for you, and it might be useful, perhaps, if you gave your views on this suggestion. It is also a suggestion which has already been discussed within the Chamber, and the Chamber approved of this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a difficult issue in the abstract to speak to, but with the greatest of respect, I would adopt Judge Trechsel's very sensible suggestion. I do think that's the very best way of proceeding. Your Honour, going to matters of the agenda, I rise now to make one application, and I believe I speak with the consensus of all Defence teams. At the moment we have another Status Conference scheduled on the 26th of March. Your Honour, it's very difficult prior to the 65 ter lists being distributed and analysed and qualitated to actually make meaningful submissions that are going to lead to further refinement in case preparation. Your Honour, what I would, with respect, suggest is that perhaps we can vacate that hearing on the 26th of April. The 21st of April -- sorry, the 26th of March, vacate that. The 21st of April we have a Status Conference scheduled which we can make far more meaningful because we would of course by that have read everybody's 65 ter list. There can be behind the scenes discussions amongst all the teams, and Your Honour, I think even at that point perhaps, it can be supplemented with an order, Defence teams and the Prosecution can give an outline flexible time estimate as to how long they will need to cross-examine each of the viva voce witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, my answer is no for the following reason: We have prepared an agenda, and we will not be able to address all the items on the agenda given the number of topics at issue. This is why we have decided to meet again on the 26th of March in order to settle the remaining items and other 65 ter issues, and the following meeting is the Pre-Defence Conference, and then the Trial Chamber will have to set the number of witnesses on the list and the time allocated to them. But before doing that, we need to have sufficient information to do so. Now, this question I've just addressed is a question which is an important question also. We are not going to let all and everyone decide on how much time he or she wishes to have for the cross-examination. That is out of the question. So we need to have some understanding of this beforehand. And if, for instance, Mr. Stojic calls a witness, I don't know, randomly, somebody who would be the Chief of Cabinet or somebody when he was minister of defence, if you have three hours to put questions to him, then we will have our questions, and how much time is the other party going to have, because three hours for you, that could amount to ten hours or six hours or eight hours. We just don't know. This is why we would like to know, and we would like know how you have decided to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and that was why I respectively -- respectfully adopted the eminently sensible suggestion of Your Learned Brother Judge Trechsel. We can't possibly even begin to give a wild guess at this juncture. The very best way may indeed be after the 65 ter lists have been circulated and discussions have taken place amongst the Defence teams. And of course the Prosecution can even, you know, ask questions and ask for some clarification. Each team can give an estimate as to how long they anticipate at this juncture of course not being privy to the statement and of course not being privy to the evidence in chief, give a rough estimate as to how long they think they will need, and then of course, Your Honour, it's for you and colleagues as a Trial Chamber to decide whether or not those estimates are reasonable or not or whether or not they need to be circumscribed depending upon your analysis and the time available for the rest of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour may I make a suggestion. I'm looking myself -- Your Honours are running today, and of course we are making such contributions as we can, but when I look at the remaining items on the agenda at pages 6 and 7, we break those items down into those aspects that also can't really usefully be discussed very far until we've got the 65 ter list and so until sometime after the 31st of March. And then when we look at what's left, I do respectfully suggest, Your Honour, that we could get through that business by 7.00 if everybody adopted reasonable economy, and then we wouldn't need to come back for a day which sounds at the moment as if it's just going to be an entire day for everybody just to finish off a small number of items that we haven't got round to finishing today. So Your Honour may I suggest that we simply crack on and finish these item on the agenda by 7.00 and then do exactly what Mr. Khan has suggested, and I do once again endorse everything that Mr. Khan has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm a bit conflicted here. I do agree with Mr. Khan that perhaps it's not necessary to have the next meeting on March 26th. In fact, I brought this to the attention to -- to the senior -- I believe it was I'll promote her for the day, Senior Legal Officer. I brought it to her attention way back. At the same time I did have a request that perhaps the April 21 date be pushed back to April 17th or 16th, somewhere around that neighbourhood. So that would be -- and I would -- I think that that would be more useful. I would also -- I also wanted to add today that if it was -- if it was possible for this 31st of March, 2008, to be pushed to April 7th. However, I understand everybody's getting a little excited and concerned. It may not be possible to have an absolute certainty on March 31st despite our best efforts. So at the very -- so we would then be asking for some leave in the future to supplement. And we're talking about some very minor changes, you know, but we're almost there, but I was advised by my colleague to make this request. It was a sensible one. She's still in the field. But in any event, I believe we can finish. I would say that if -- if we were to dispense with the next meeting on the 26th, then at least perhaps the Trial Chamber, you know, would ask a commitment from the Defence to absolutely meet and if at all possible to get back to the Trial Chamber with some sort of a status report as far as where we are, perhaps supplementing or altering our current projections and maybe even, you know, taking on the first step toward what Judge Trechsel had indicated as far as trying to figure out how much hours. We can just put initials for now, but at least it might give everybody an indication on the Bench how much time. Because I think once we see each other's list, some witnesses may go by the wayside. But anyway, I do concur with Mr. Khan, but I'm just one voice in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I join in the position put forward by my colleagues, although I understood your example -- your proposal or the agenda that you put forward earlier on as being a discussion of principle. That is to say this point on the agenda was allocation of time, cross, and the Prosecution and other Defences. So regardless of the fact that I agree with the arguments put forward by my learned friends with respect to calendar, we could discuss some matters in due course later on, because we'll be able to say more things and better define them. And I wouldn't be opposed to discussing the principle of cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, Mr. Coric's Defence? So as far as cross-examination is concerned, what's your view?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please counsel. Could you speak into the microphone, please? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I agree with everything my colleagues have said thus far today. I have nothing more to add. As I said, I was told that I couldn't be heard. I agree with what my colleagues have said and I have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps it's an opportune moment for the Prosecution to tell us how much time they need for cross-examination, because they are now in the position that we were in two years ago. So is it in the ratio of one to one or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, let's imagine a situation in which a witness has two hours. Let's say there are two hours for the examination-in-chief and other Defence counsel need two to three hours to put questions to the witness. That would take five hours. What would you do then? How much time would you need? I mean, this is in the abstract, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As a basic principle, Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask for only as much time as was used in direct examination of a witness. Therefore, any cross-examination by any accused would not be computed, but certainly we would ask for -- if there was two hours of direct examination, then we would ask for at least two hours of cross-examination. That also, Your Honour, leads into or leads back into the problem raised earlier by Mr. Karnavas in that if any accused were to during their examination of a witness actually question the witness not actually in cross-examination but in direct examination, that would also beg the question whether the Prosecution would be allowed additional time to compensate for such direct examination. But in conclusion on this, Your Honour, the -- during the Prosecution case, the flexible system employed by the Chamber did work well in which the rule of thumb was as much time as the examination-in-chief was, so much time was granted for -- allocated for cross-examination, and of course it was allowed flexibly in that in certain instances more time was allocated as was required, and then obviously in some instances less time was used by the questioning party. And, Your Honour, then if the Prosecution may just make one further observation at this stage, and that is that the Prosecution would also at this stage feel that it's appropriate that the examination or the

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: conclusion of all examinations by the Defence, whether as examination-in-chief or examination -- cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be extremely clear and to avoid any misunderstanding, let's assume that the Petkovic Defence examines a witness during two hours. Then the other Defence counsel takes five minutes, 30 minutes, nothing, one hour, two hours. You, as far as you're concerned, would only ask for two hours. You would ask for precisely the same time as used for examination-in-chief. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honour. We would ask for the examination chief time. And for those accused who were cross-examining a witness, that time would not be computed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps as you are almost standing still -- stand up again. Mr. Kruger, do you have a view as to an issue discussed by a number of Defence teams as to whether you consider it useful or even necessary that we hold another 65 ter Conference on the -- what was it, the 16th of this month -- 26th, or would you also say it is superfluous?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly there are items on the agenda which can only be discussed in very general terms unless we are provided with the 65 ter list, but certainly we can discuss those points in basic terms, and I don't think, however, being quite frank, that it's possible to cover all of those points in the time left. So at this stage I foresee that there will be some time needed subsequent to this unless we are all very disciplined, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I may be allowed to make one observation? The Defence of General Petkovic, like all the other Defence teams in these proceedings, had the right to cross-examination up to the time of one-sixth of the time needed by the Prosecution for the examination-in-chief. Now, I consider that the same rule should apply in the Defence cases when the Defence is conducting the examination-in-chief. That is to say that the Prosecution should have the right to one-sixth of the time used by a Defence team for its examination-in-chief. And I'd also like to appeal to you to be flexible, to allow the Prosecutor to have a little more time sometimes than that one-sixth if they need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not want to take the floor earlier on because we were just discussing whether or not we were going to discuss the matter in first place, but since we've started the discussion my proposal is identical to the one put forward by my learned friend Ms. Alaburic. And I would like to add a point in favour of it, in favour of why. The Prosecution advocated at the beginning of the trial, and it knew at the time that the trial had two stages, so they advocated equal treatment. That is to say if the Prosecution has two hours then the Defence, according to their interpretation, one Defence team regardless of Rule 82 to which each accused has the right to its own case, should have the same amount of time, and the Trial Chamber accepted that. So we have already established the principle during the Prosecution case, and we had 180 witnesses, I believe, based on that principle and governed by that principle. If the Prosecution had two hours, then the Defence had two hours. So if we transpose that and have the same principle reign for the Defence case, and we've already discussed this earlier on that the Defence are calling -- the Defence team calling the witness has time for examination in chief, five accused plus the Prosecution have the right to a cross-examination, and they can divide up that time with the proviso - and I'd like to add this - because our interests might not be identical with the five accused. I know this sounds absurd, but the interest need not be identical, so I'm very flexible, and I think that the Prosecutor when he has sound reason should be allowed a little more time. It's quite obvious something that Judge Antonetti said a moment ago based on experience, and I do have experience myself, that very rarely will the other Defence teams have any more important questions to raise with the witness than the Defence team that called that witness, and I do believe that to be the case thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken due note of your requests, and we'll consider the matter. Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Just a technical question. I can't cooperate with my Defence counsel, he's a little far away, but bearing in mind what Judge Prandler was saying, objectively speaking the Defence in the -- used a little more time than the Prosecution during the first stage of the trial, and if we look at all these figures then it's a fifth of the time. So the correction that was made by Ms. Alaburic would roughly go up to a fifth of the time to be used in the cross-examination. The Prosecution in comparison to the Defence time if we wish to retain the principle that was used in the first stage of the trial as put forward by Judge Prandler. So that's just a technical proposal that can be used as an orientation in how the stage two of the trial is to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll take your comments into account when we deliberate on the matter. I'm going to try and proceed very quickly on the following points. Point 4, the number of witnesses. We've already dealt with this. You've given us information about this. So if you like, we'll move on to the following point on the agenda, common witnesses. Mr. Karnavas said that there would be common witnesses. The other Defence counsel said that this was news to them, but they had already considered having joint or common witnesses. I understand that there will be two types of expert witnesses. There will be at least one military expert witness, and there will be an expert on constitutional matters. There maybe other experts. I'm not sure. Mr. Karnavas, when it comes to experts, have you seen or met other experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Mr. President. One expert will be dealing with economic issues. There's been quite a bit of discussion concerning, for instance, what was -- what were the responsibilities of the state government at the time, whether it was functioning and so on and so forth. Also, there have been lots of testimony from Prosecution witnesses, primarily I believe it was Tomljanovich and some others, as to what these laws were, and what we want to do is present to the Trial Chamber some expertise that would allow the Trial Chamber to understand the complete picture from an expert as far as what was the state's responsibilities, how this particular system functioned because it's quite different than other systems because Yugoslavia did have a sort of a unique system, and then as the war came and the republics broke apart, that becomes rather relevant. And also an evaluation of all relevant jurisprudence, if I may use that term, drafted by the HVO, the executive authority concerning economic matters to show exactly to the Trial Chamber what the functions were and to show that there was this gap as a result of the war and they filled in this gap, and you'll see that other municipalities or other regions were doing the same thing. You know, they were doing -- taking some measures as a result of Sarajevo being under siege and so on and so forth. The other expert deals with another matter. I'm not quite firm on that. It's a much shorter expertise. I hesitate at this point in time because I'm not absolutely certain to divulge what it is because I'm still at the stage of trying to make those arrangements, but that will -- that decision will be made within the next few days. But in any event, those are the expertise, and course we do know about the constitutional expert. And -- let me see. If I may have one moment, Your Honour. I believe -- yes, and there is one other expert, I should say, Your Honour. That has to do with demographics. Again, you know, I haven't consulted with my colleagues because they've all been busy, but we heard the testimony of the OTP employee/analyst/expert Ewa Tabeau, and she presented certain evidence here and we have consulted with an expert who's testified in this Tribunal on numerous occasions. She's from Belgrade, and at this point in time we're in communication with the Prosecution to allow her access to documents. It has been done in the past. This is a procedure that has been done which under a controlled environment she would look over the documents herself and anticipate having a short report by this expert. So those are the three experts that we anticipate in addition to the constitutional expert. And as far as the military expert we don't have anyone. We don't know who else is coming. And if I can assist the Trial Chamber with anything else with regard to experts, please feel free to fire away questions. If not, I'll just sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we can see that there will be a minimum of five expert witnesses. And this brings me to point 7, time needed for translations and disclosure of expert reports. I suppose that your experts will prepare short or longer reports. These reports will have to be translated into English and handed over to the Prosecutor for the Prosecution to respond, and for the Chamber to decide on the quality of the expert and on the way we should proceed. The earlier you have these reports the better it will be for everyone. Let me now move on to 92 bis and 92 ter statements. Several of you have told us that you will use 92 bis or 92 ter proceedings or procedures. Statements will need to be taken. That can be done in two ways, either through a representative of the registry, a presiding officer appointed by the registrar, or that may be done by the country where the person resides through its judicial authorities. I don't know at what stage you are. I know that Mr. Praljak has 120 92 bis witnesses lined up. Have you started working on this? Have you started, Mr. Kovacic, taking statements from these people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the exception of some five to ten witnesses, I don't have the precise number at present, all these statements have already been certified based on Rule 92 ter (A) -- excuse me, no. According to the rules of the states in which the statements were taken. In Croatia it's the law on the public notaries that regulates this. So these statements have been certified by notaries public. In Bosnia previously there were no notaries public so this was done with the local courts in the so-called out of trial, out of court proceedings. However, now a law on notaries public has been passed in Bosnia-Herzegovina similar to other European laws, so from that point onwards the statements were certified by notaries public. We have already done and lot of this work, and then we realised that technically it would be a far greater job if this was done through the registry, so we did this in the quickest and easiest way we could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So there's no problem on that matter. Item 9, translation of documents listed on the 65 ter (G) list. The summaries will be translated in due course. What's really crucial here is what's related to documents that you'll show your witnesses. These documents need to be translated. Is there any problem in that respect? Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, there is. Thank you for your concern. You have been informed of this through various submissions. One more decision is expected. I will not speak about this in public, but the fact is that our Defence case has run into problems with translation. I have to say that we are deeply dissatisfied with this. The registry will not like my saying this, but I have to say it, because ultimately the organisation of this Tribunal and the internal policy of the registry are, I am deeply convinced, contrary to the basic rights of the accused in these proceedings, especially the provisions of the Statute saying that the accused must have adequate support, including translation. I don't know how this will develop further. We are submitting documents on a daily basis, and we shall see what happens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you know that the Chamber has considered the matter. There have been a number of meetings with the Chamber's legal officer. We haven't had any hearings these past few weeks, that's right, but I've been thinking and working on this case constantly, just as my fellow Judges. What the CLSS has told us is that they can translate 200 pages a month for Mr. Praljak. That's all they can do. They told me that they have already translated 2.000 pages for you. That's the way things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The facts are beyond dispute more or less, but when it comes to the number of pages, this information means nothing to me. They are a bureaucratic institution counting pages and lines. I won't go into any issues of the standards as to what constitutes a line or page. What I'm interested in are the documents, as are you, Your Honours. You are not going to ask me how many pages a document has, you are going to ask for a document and that is the only realistic criterion. But I have no influence on this. They can decide that their maximum is 2.000 pages or 250 pages. I have no way of influencing this quite simply. The basic problem is that issue was raised when you were the Pre-Trial Judge at a time when the Accused Praljak was mounting his own Defence case, and there were some 60 DVDs with documents he assumed he would need. Over the following few months -- I don't want to make a mistake, but about 800 pages were translated, and the rest was returned to us and we were told it would not be translated. That was when the registry was first informed of the fact that there were many documents here. And then when this Defence case started we all knew that there would be a great many documents. The registry first said that they can translate only exhibits. This is absurd because it's the Trial Chamber that decides what is going to be an exhibit or not. And for me to tender a document into evidence it has to be translated, and that's where the major problem arose. And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we are aware of the problem. What is your solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been corresponding with the registry and I proposed out-sourcing, engaging external services. The registry says that these have been fully used. Let the registry then approve a budget for me and I will do it. But it's not just matter of financing it's also a matter of management. If I have to employ two or three translation agencies, I need a man who will keep track of all the documents, what has been sent to whom, when, what has to be paid, when, and so on and so forth. It requires a full-time clerk, and I don't have the resources to engage one. And this is also not in our job description on the basis of which the registry approves the number of people in our team. So that with all goodwill and with -- with certain financial resources, the problem can be solved, but we have neither the finances nor the people, nor the manpower. I have not asked the registry for money to do this because I don't want to take this burden upon myself, but if they have cannot increase the number of documents they can translate, let them do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you talked about thousands of documents, and if I remember correctly, mention was made of Muslims who had been relocated and that you have thousands of documents related to that. You may have documents from the municipal authorities, certificates, et cetera. If you have thousands such documents, you only need to have two or three such documents translated into English, and you do not need to have the other documents, the hundreds or thousands of documents that say the same things about these Muslims who were given another flat or house. You might have to decide on your priorities when it comes to all these documents. I remember that the Prlic Defence told us that the Croatisation of the streets -- street names was not a fact, contrary to what the Prosecutor said, and we had been shown countless documents that seemed, and I insist, that seemed to show that the street names had been changed in another spirit. And we were shown several documents testifying to this. It might not have been necessary. One or two documents may have been sufficient. That's an example. That's a case where you only need one or two documents, and you do not need to have all the other documents that say exactly the same thing translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are, of course, keeping this in mind. When we are dealing with documents of the same type more or less, we did precisely what you suggest. We chose two or three typical documents. We put the rest aside. But of course I have to be cautious, because what I don't include in Rule 65 ter (G) in that list I will not be allowed to use, so I have to leave some room for myself to be on the safe side. So I have to put the documents on the list in spite of the fact that they haven't been translated. In this way we have eliminated a certain number of documents from the translation list, but there are many documents which we believe at present are the only documents of that type and that we have to translate them, and that the other Defence teams do not have any similar documents. It has, true to say, been a little easier for us since we were informed by Your Honours that we don't have to have all the documents on our 65 ter list translated already, so we will be able to check the documents of the other Defence teams, and we may be able to reduce the number of documents, but according to what I know, this will not be a dramatic reduction; although, it will contribute to reducing the number of documents. Secondly, we have already reduced our translation requests to -- in a large measure over the past few months, because every document we wanted to include on our list is one where we first looked to see if there were translations already available from other sources, and in many cases we did manage to find these. We may have erroneously sent something for translation which has already been translated, but the number of such errors is negligible, I believe. In any case, what I'm trying to say is the following: If you give us sufficient time to make an effort and see whether we have any reserves after we have filed our 65 ter lists, this will mitigate our problem. We'll be able to file our lists. That's what matters. And then some documents will be translated in time, and then if there are still problems we will seek a solution. One problem will remain, Your Honours, and the registry has been evading it from the outset. A year and a half I had my first meeting in this respect. The witness summaries have been translated but not the witness statements, and under 92 bis we are counting on about 120 witnesses. These have not been translated. Our understanding is that the registry will accept them for translation when the Chamber accepts my witness list according to 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you said you had 120 92 bis witnesses. Is that absolutely necessary? Of course I don't know these witnesses, but can't you reduce that figure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think so. I don't think I can. You will see the lists, and they are subject to your decision that's one thing. Secondly, among these 120 there are a significant number of witnesses - I can't tell you the number off the top of my head - who come -- who fall into the pattern of conduct category. I think that's Rule 93. If someone is attempting inter alia in a defence case to demonstrate a pattern of conduct, and this of course speaks to mens rea, it's not enough to bring two, three, or five people who will say, "Yes, I know the accused. He was a good and honourable man." But that's useless. If, however, you demonstrate over a certain period of time throughout the period of the war, from the very beginning of the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and the war started in Croatia, and General Praljak started his wartime activities in Croatia, if I'm able to demonstrate a consistent pattern of conduct on the part of the accused with several dozen statements of people who say, "Yes, I was with him in the war in such and such a place and such and such a time and this was how he behaved, this is how things were done. This is where refugees were fed, this is where neighbours were fed, this is where soldiers were punished for shooting their Serbian neighbour's cat," and so on and so forth, I cannot show such a consistent pattern of conduct with five, ten, or twelve witnesses. These are all relatively brief witness statements, but how can I deal with these issues if I don't show consistency over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give you the floor again. We have acknowledged this. We shall ask the translation services to translate 120 statements as a matter of some urgency. This is important. This is what we will ask the translation services to do. Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
